If you had told a developer in early 2020 that by the end of 2026 most of their peers would use AI every working day, that software agents would open pull requests, and that a model would be better than a PhD-level human baseline on science questions while still fumbling an analog clock, they would have asked what you were smoking.

Well. It's mid-November 2026.

So let's do something we rarely do in this industry: stop, zoom out, and measure how far AI has actually travelled in six and a half years. Not hype. Numbers, milestones, and one uncomfortable pattern in the data that I think every developer should think about.

And at the end, there's a very concrete story about what all this means for a tool millions of people use, and a deadline that is 15 days away.

First, a correction: AI didn't "arrive" in 2020

Dev.to will eat me alive if I skip this. AI research is decades old. Deep learning broke through in 2012, and the Transformer architecture dropped in 2017.

But 2020 is the year the curve bent for everyone else. GPT-3 showed that if you scale a Transformer far enough, you get something that follows instructions from a handful of examples, with no task-specific training. That one idea (you can "program" a model with text) is the root of almost everything that followed. So I'm using 2020 as year zero of the era we're all living in.

The six-year timeline

Year The moment Why developers cared
2020 GPT-3 arrives (mid-year). AlphaFold 2 dominates the CASP14 protein-folding challenge (late-year). Few-shot prompting is born. And AI cracks a 50-year-old science problem.
2021 DALL·E (Jan). GitHub Copilot technical preview (Jun). For the first time, AI lives inside the editor.
2022 DALL·E 2, open-weights Stable Diffusion, then ChatGPT on Nov 30. Image generation goes open source. ChatGPT turns "AI" into a text box anyone can use; analysts estimated ~100M users within about two months.
2023 GPT-4, Claude, Llama 2 (open weights). Multimodal and long-context models; RAG becomes a default architecture; "prompt engineer" becomes a job title (briefly).
2024 Sora preview. Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry both honour AI-related work. Legitimacy. AI is now science, not just product.
2025 Reasoning models. DeepSeek-R1 open weights (Jan). Terminal and IDE coding agents go mainstream. Models "think" before answering. Costs fall. Developers start delegating, not just autocompleting.
2026 Agents inside everyday workflows. Stanford's AI Index says capability is accelerating, not plateauing. The question changes from "can it do it?" to "can I trust it, and who's accountable?"

What the numbers say

Timelines are fun; surveys are honest. Stack Overflow has been asking developers about AI since 2023, and the trajectory is steep.

Developers using AI tools (Stack Overflow):

2023 2024 2025 2026
44% 62% 79% only ~17% say they don't use AI tools at work

AI agents are the faster story. In the 2025 survey, 31% of respondents used agents. A smaller pulse survey in April 2026 found agent use had almost doubled to 59%, with Claude Code usage among agent users rising from 41% to 55%.

And outside our bubble, Lightcast's read of the Stanford data shows 2.5% of all US job postings now mention AI skills: up 55% in a year and roughly 300% over a decade.

So: massive adoption. Done, right? Not quite.

The uncomfortable pattern: usage up, trust down

Here's the part that doesn't fit the hype narrative.

  • In 2025, 46% of developers said they distrust AI output, versus 33% who trust it. Only 3% said they "highly trust" it.
  • In the 2026 survey, nearly half trust AI output when they can easily verify it. Just 6.6% would trust it with an important decision.
  • The most common frustration in 2025: solutions that are "almost right, but not quite."
  • Governance is lagging: only 24% of respondents said their employer had published approved AI tools or guidance.

I'd argue this is the defining dynamic of 2026: AI has become infrastructure faster than it has become trustworthy. We use it constantly and check it constantly.

Stanford's 2026 AI Index captures the same weirdness from the capability side: models now beat human baselines on PhD-level science questions, yet still fail at tasks like reading an analog clock. Researchers call this jagged intelligence: brilliant peaks, baffling potholes.

My takeaway (opinion, not data): the most valuable developer skill of the next few years isn't prompting. It's verification: writing tests, reading diffs, designing systems where a wrong-but-plausible answer gets caught.

The quiet shift nobody is tweeting about: AI left the data center

In 2020, running a serious neural network meant renting GPUs and calling an API. That model (your data goes up, the answer comes down, and you pay per call) defined the first half of this era.

The second half is different. Thanks to WebAssembly, WebGPU, and runtimes like ONNX Runtime Web, a browser tab can now run real models locally:

import * as ort from "onnxruntime-web";

// Simplified: load a model once, cache it, run inference on-device
const session = await ort.InferenceSession.create("/models/segmenter.onnx", {
  executionProviders: ["wasm"], // or "webgpu" where supported
});

const result = await session.run({ input: imageTensor });
// Nothing was uploaded. No API key. No per-call bill.

Why this matters:

  • Privacy: sensitive data never leaves the device.
  • Cost: inference runs on the user's hardware, so there are no per-image credits.
  • Latency and availability: after the first download there is no round trip, and some tools work offline.
  • Longevity: your tool can't be switched off because someone else's API changed pricing.

That last point just became very real for millions of people.

Case study: the end of an era

For years, remove.bg was the answer to "how do I remove a background?" It popularised one-click AI background removal and was a textbook example of the cloud-API era.

Now its standalone website is closing on December 1, 2026, with the functionality moving into Canva (which has owned it since 2021). Reporting based on remove.bg's own FAQ says the closure is at 9:00 CET, unused pay-as-you-go credits expire, and the self-serve API moves to Leonardo.Ai (also Canva-owned). If you rely on it, export your usage reports and invoices before the cutoff.

There's a lesson here that has nothing to do with any single company: if your workflow depends on someone else's server, it has an expiry date you don't control.

If you're already in the Canva ecosystem, Canva is the official successor and will be fine for you. But if you want something that doesn't ask for an account or a credit card, or send your photos anywhere, read on.

Meet APIC: the on-device approach, in practice

Full disclosure: I built APIC, so weigh my opinion accordingly. But everything below is verifiable in about 60 seconds, which is exactly why I'm comfortable showing it to a room full of skeptical developers.

👉 apic-studio.vercel.app

APIC (Advanced Image Processing Center) is a free, browser-based photo editor where the AI runs on your device. No upload. No credits. No account required to edit or export (there's an optional Google sign-in, nothing more).

Background removal, the remove.bg use case

  • On-device AI cut-out with three model sizes: Light (~5 MB, built for phones), Fast (~44 MB), and Maximum (~176 MB, multi-pass, best on a PC). Models download once and are cached.
  • A Restore / Erase brush to fix hair, fur and awkward edges, plus one-click replacement with white, black or a blurred copy of your photo.
  • Full-resolution output as transparent PNG or WebP.
  • Batch mode: remove backgrounds, resize, compress and convert many images, then download one ZIP.

And because I got tired of juggling ten tabs, it's eleven tools in one

  • Remove Object: paint over a person, sign or blemish; inpainting runs locally (MI-GAN ~28 MB, or LaMa ~208 MB for big, complex fills).
  • AI upscale (2x / 4x) with Real-ESRGAN.
  • Compress to an exact file size ("under 200 KB" for that upload form), resize, and convert between PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, BMP, ICO, PDF and PSD, with HEIC photos accepted as input.
  • Pro colour tools: histogram, RGB curves, HSL mixer, 3-way grading, and 3D LUT (.cube) export for DaVinci Resolve, Premiere and Photoshop.
  • Social presets for 15+ networks with safe-zone guides; Layers with blend modes and PSD import/export; Hide area to blur or pixelate faces, plates and card numbers before you share.
  • A Windows app that runs fully offline, no account needed.

The honest trade-offs (because you'd find them anyway):

  • The first run of any AI tool downloads its model, so it's slower once and fast afterwards.
  • The heaviest models are best on a desktop-class machine. On phones, use Light.
  • It's a browser tool, not a replacement for Photoshop's full ecosystem.
  • I'm one developer shipping this, not a 500-person company. Feedback genuinely shapes the roadmap.

Try it with your hardest photo

Don't test it on a clean studio shot. Take the image remove.bg struggled with (wispy hair, glass, a busy background) and run it through APIC's Remove BG tab on Maximum. Use the Restore brush if needed. If it doesn't hold up, tell me where it failed. If it does, you've just saved yourself a subscription.

Make it your default (it takes 20 seconds)

With 15 days left on the old default, now is the moment to build a new habit:

  1. Open apic-studio.vercel.app and drop in a photo.
  2. Bookmark it and pin the tab, so "remove background" now means one click on your own bookmarks bar.
  3. Send it to the one person in your team, family or client list who still says "just use remove.bg."
  4. Tell me what's missing: a comment below, or find me on GitHub / dev.to. I read everything.

(I also wrote a shorter, practical guide on the remove.bg shutdown specifically: remove.bg Is Shutting Down — Here's a Free, No-Upload Alternative.)

So, how much AI is there in six years?

Started as a research demo behind a waitlist in 2020. By 2026 it's in the editor, the terminal, the job postings, the Nobel Prizes, the survey data, and increasingly, in your browser tab, running on your own hardware.

The next six years won't be about who has the biggest model. They'll be about three questions:

  1. Can I verify it? (trust)
  2. Who controls it? (open weights, on-device, no kill switch)
  3. Does it respect the user? (privacy by architecture, not by policy)

The tools that win on all three won't need a marketing budget. They'll just be the ones people quietly never switch away from.

I'm betting on that. Come try APIC, and tell me where I'm wrong.

Your turn: what was your "oh, this changes everything" AI moment between 2020 and 2026: GPT-3, Copilot, ChatGPT, or something else? Drop it in the comments. 👇

Sources: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025 · Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026 coverage · Stanford HAI AI Index 2026 · Lightcast · remove.bg shutdown reporting

articles.title: Swagger UI is from 2011. It’s Time to Upgrade to Scalar.
articles.description: You've built a modern backend with TypeScript, NestJS, or Fastify. Clean architecture, type-safe...
articles.body_html:
You've built a modern backend with TypeScript, NestJS, or Fastify. Clean architecture, type-safe APIs, and everything working perfectly.

Then someone opens your /docs endpoint.

And there it is. The same old Swagger UI.

Don't get me wrong. Swagger UI is great and has served developers for years. But API documentation can look and feel much better.

That's where Scalar comes in.

What Is Scalar?

Scalar is an open-source API documentation tool that gives your OpenAPI documentation a cleaner, more modern interface.

Think of it as Swagger UI, but with a better developer experience.

Here's what makes it interesting:

  • Modern UI: Clean layout, dark mode, and customizable themes.
  • Built-in API client: Test endpoints directly without switching to Postman.
  • Code snippets: Generate request examples in JavaScript, Python, Go, and more.
  • Authentication: Support for Bearer tokens, API keys, and other OpenAPI security schemes.
  • OpenAPI support: Works with your existing OpenAPI specifications.

And the best part?

You don't need to change your backend or rewrite your API schemas.

Swagger UI vs. Scalar

Here's a quick comparison:

Feature Swagger UI Scalar
UI Design Traditional accordion layout Modern, clean interface
Dark Mode Requires customization Built-in
API Testing Basic Try it out Integrated API client
Code Snippets Configurable request snippets Multiple languages and clients
Authentication Bearer, API keys, OAuth2 Bearer, API keys, OAuth2
Search Endpoint filtering Integrated reference search
Customization CSS and configuration Built-in themes and configuration
OpenAPI 3.1 Supported Supported
Open Source Yes Yes

Both tools do the job, but Scalar focuses more on the overall developer experience, especially when exploring and testing APIs.

How Easy Is It to Integrate?

If you're using Fastify with @fastify/swagger already configured, it's just a few lines.

Install Scalar:

npm install @scalar/fastify-api-reference

Register it in your Fastify application:

await fastify.register(
  import('@scalar/fastify-api-reference'),
  {
    routePrefix: '/docs',
    configuration: {
      theme: 'purple',
    },
  }
);

Now open:

http://localhost:3000/docs

That's it. Your existing OpenAPI specification now has a modern documentation interface.

Scalar also supports NestJS, Express, Next.js, and other frameworks.

Should You Replace Swagger UI?

Not necessarily.

Swagger UI is still actively maintained and supports OpenAPI 3.1, authentication, and interactive requests.

Scalar simply offers a different, more polished experience for exploring and testing APIs.

If you're happy with Swagger UI, there's no reason to rush.

But if you want better-looking, developer-friendly API documentation without much effort, Scalar is definitely worth trying.

Final Thoughts

We spend hours improving our backend architecture, performance, and code quality.

Why not give the same attention to our API documentation?

A great API deserves a great developer experience.

Give Scalar a try on your next project.

What do you use for API documentation — Swagger UI, Scalar, or something else?

articles.title: TypeScript `Omit` vs `Pick` vs `Exclude` in 2026: Choosing the Right Utility Type Without Guessing
articles.description: Stop confusing Pick, Omit, and Exclude. Learn when each TypeScript utility type applies, why Omit silently accepts typos, and how to enforce type safety with strict variants.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript Omit vs Pick vs Exclude in 2026: Choosing the Right Utility Type Without Guessing

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers reach for Omit when they need Pick, apply Exclude to object types that need Omit, and ship code that compiles cleanly but accepts any string literal as a property name. TypeScript provides six property-manipulation utilities that look similar but operate on fundamentally different input shapes. The confusion costs hours in debugging sessions where the compiler stays silent while the runtime produces undefined values.

The root problem is naming. Pick and Omit transform object types. Exclude and Extract filter union types. No visual or naming convention signals which category each utility belongs to, so developers test by trial until the compiler accepts the syntax. The correct approach groups utilities by input shape first, then checks whether the operation adds or removes members.

Key Takeaways

  • Pick and Omit operate on object types by selecting or removing properties; Exclude and Extract operate on union types by filtering members.
  • Omit accepts any string literal without checking if the property exists, allowing typos to compile successfully while producing incorrect types.
  • Decision framework: check the input shape (object vs union) before choosing the utility, then decide whether the operation should include or remove members.
  • Strict variants from type-zoo (PickStrict, OmitStrict) enforce property existence at compile time, catching typos and refactoring oversights.
  • Object utilities preserve structure and return new object types; union utilities return new unions with fewer or different members.

Pick vs Omit: Object Property Selection

Pick<Type, Keys> constructs a new type by selecting a subset of properties from an existing object type. The operation requires two inputs: the source object type and a string literal or union of string literals naming the properties to extract. TypeScript introduced Pick in version 2.1 alongside Partial, Readonly, and Record.

interface UserAccount {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  passwordHash: string;
  createdAt: Date;
  lastLogin: Date;
  preferences: Record<string, unknown>;
}

type PublicProfile = Pick<UserAccount, "id" | "email" | "createdAt">;

const profile: PublicProfile = {
  id: "usr_123",
  email: "user@example.com",
  createdAt: new Date("2026-01-15"),
};

The pattern fits API response types where the backend returns a subset of database columns. GraphQL resolvers often return fragments that match a Pick type exactly. The alternative approach requires duplicating property definitions across multiple interfaces, which creates maintenance burden when field types change.

Omit<Type, Keys> constructs a new type by removing specified properties from an existing object type. TypeScript added Omit in version 3.5 as the inverse of Pick. The operation accepts the same input types but produces the complement set of properties.

type UserUpdatePayload = Omit<UserAccount, "id" | "createdAt">;

function updateUser(userId: string, updates: UserUpdatePayload) {
  // Implementation accepts all fields except immutable ones
}

The comparison reveals a structural difference beyond inclusion versus exclusion. Pick forces developers to list exactly what the new type contains. Omit forces developers to list what the new type excludes. The cognitive load shifts based on whether the remaining properties or the excluded properties form a shorter list.

Utility Input type Operation Output Use case
Pick Object type Select named properties New object type with subset API responses, public interfaces
Omit Object type Remove named properties New object type without exclusions Update payloads, sensitive data removal

The decision between Pick and Omit depends on which list is shorter and which intent is clearer. A type that needs 2 properties from a 10-property interface uses Pick. A type that needs 8 properties from a 10-property interface uses Omit. Neither choice affects runtime behavior or compilation output, but the shorter list reduces maintenance surface area.

TypeScript utility types decision matrix

Exclude vs Extract: Union Type Filtering

Exclude<UnionType, ExcludedMembers> constructs a new union by removing all members from UnionType that are assignable to ExcludedMembers. TypeScript introduced Exclude in version 2.8 as part of a set of conditional type utilities. The operation works on union types exclusively and fails when applied to object types.

type HTTPMethod = "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH";
type ReadOnlyMethod = Exclude<HTTPMethod, "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH">;

function fetchData(method: ReadOnlyMethod, url: string) {
  // Only GET requests compile
}

Extract<Type, Union> constructs a new union by selecting all members from Type that are assignable to Union. The operation inverts Exclude by keeping matching members instead of removing them. Both utilities appeared in the same TypeScript release as complementary tools.

type MutatingMethod = Extract<HTTPMethod, "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE" | "PATCH">;

function modifyResource(method: MutatingMethod, url: string, body: unknown) {
  // GET fails to compile
}

The confusion between object utilities and union utilities stems from overlapping terminology. "Exclude" and "Omit" both remove things. "Extract" and "Pick" both select things. The critical distinction is input shape: object types have named properties, union types have discrete members. TypeScript enforces this boundary at compile time but provides no naming convention to signal the category.

The pattern fits discriminated unions where runtime logic branches on a subset of possible values. State machines often use Extract to constrain valid transitions from a given state. Event handlers use Exclude to prevent certain event types from reaching sensitive code paths.

Utility Input type Operation Output Use case
Exclude Union type Remove matching members New union without exclusions Restricting valid values, state machines
Extract Union type Keep matching members New union with only matches Filtering event types, permission checks

Real-World Code Examples: API Response Types

Backend services often return nested JSON structures where different endpoints expose different subsets of the same entity. TypeScript utility types model these variations without duplicating property definitions. Consider a user service that stores comprehensive account data but exposes sanitized versions through public APIs.

interface DatabaseUser {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  passwordHash: string;
  passwordSalt: string;
  totpSecret: string | null;
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
  deletedAt: Date | null;
  emailVerified: boolean;
  roles: Array<"admin" | "moderator" | "user">;
  loginAttempts: number;
  lastLoginIp: string | null;
  preferences: {
    theme: "light" | "dark";
    notifications: boolean;
  };
}

type PublicUserProfile = Pick<
  DatabaseUser,
  "id" | "email" | "emailVerified" | "createdAt" | "preferences"
>;

type AdminUserView = Omit<DatabaseUser, "passwordHash" | "passwordSalt" | "totpSecret">;

type UserUpdateRequest = Partial<
  Pick<DatabaseUser, "email" | "preferences">
>;

type AuthenticationResponse = Pick<DatabaseUser, "id" | "email" | "roles"> & {
  token: string;
  expiresAt: Date;
};

The composition demonstrates layering: Pick extracts the base structure, Partial makes fields optional for update operations, and intersection types add authentication metadata. Each derived type maintains a single source of truth for property shapes while modeling different access patterns.

Role-based filtering uses union utilities to constrain valid permission sets. The backend defines an exhaustive permission list as a union type, then uses Extract to model role-specific capabilities.

type Permission =
  | "users:read"
  | "users:write"
  | "users:delete"
  | "posts:read"
  | "posts:write"
  | "posts:delete"
  | "analytics:read"
  | "settings:write";

type UserPermissions = Extract<Permission, `users:${string}`>;
type PostPermissions = Extract<Permission, `posts:${string}`>;
type ReadOnlyPermissions = Extract<Permission, `${string}:read`>;

function checkPermission(
  userRole: "admin" | "moderator" | "user",
  required: Permission
): boolean {
  const rolePermissions: Record<string, Permission[]> = {
    admin: [
      "users:read", "users:write", "users:delete",
      "posts:read", "posts:write", "posts:delete",
      "analytics:read", "settings:write"
    ],
    moderator: [
      "users:read", "posts:read", "posts:write", "posts:delete"
    ],
    user: ["posts:read"]
  };

  return rolePermissions[userRole].includes(required);
}

The pattern works because Extract with template literal types filters by pattern matching. The result maintains type safety while avoiding string manipulation at runtime. Frontend code uses these derived types to conditionally render UI elements based on user permissions.

TypeScript utility types in production code

The Silent Bug: Why Omit Doesn't Catch Typos

Omit accepts any string literal in its second type parameter without verifying that the property exists on the source type. TypeScript designed this behavior intentionally to support mapped types and conditional logic, but the permissiveness creates a maintenance hazard. A typo in the excluded property list compiles successfully and produces an incorrect output type.

interface ApiResponse {
  data: unknown;
  status: number;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
  timestamp: Date;
}

// Typo: "header" instead of "headers"
type CleanResponse = Omit<ApiResponse, "header">;

const response: CleanResponse = {
  data: { userId: 123 },
  status: 200,
  headers: { "content-type": "application/json" }, // Still required
  timestamp: new Date(),
};

The code compiles without warnings. CleanResponse still contains the headers property because Omit silently ignored the nonexistent header property. The bug surfaces only when downstream code expects headers to be absent and receives an unexpected value at runtime. The compiler provides no indication that the exclusion list contains an invalid property name.

Refactoring compounds the issue. When a property name changes in the source interface, Omit calls that reference the old name continue to compile. The type system cannot detect that an excluded property no longer exists because Omit treats the exclusion list as an open set of string literals rather than a constrained subset of known properties.

interface ApiResponse {
  data: unknown;
  status: number;
  responseHeaders: Record<string, string>; // Renamed from "headers"
  timestamp: Date;
}

// Stale reference compiles successfully
type CleanResponse = Omit<ApiResponse, "headers">;

const response: CleanResponse = {
  data: { userId: 123 },
  status: 200,
  responseHeaders: { "content-type": "application/json" },
  timestamp: new Date(),
};

The workaround requires strict variants that check property existence at compile time. The type-zoo package provides OmitStrict, PickStrict, and similar utilities that fail compilation when property names do not exist on the source type. These variants add a constraint that maps the exclusion list to actual keys.

import { OmitStrict } from "type-zoo";

interface ApiResponse {
  data: unknown;
  status: number;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
  timestamp: Date;
}

// Compilation error: "header" does not exist on ApiResponse
type CleanResponse = OmitStrict<ApiResponse, "header">;

The tradeoff is explicit. Standard Omit supports dynamic property exclusion and conditional types at the cost of safety. Strict variants enforce correctness but require all excluded properties to exist in the source type. Teams must choose between flexibility and type safety based on codebase size and refactoring frequency. For more on union filtering, see TypeScript Exclude vs Extract: Union Type Filters Explained.

Practical Decision Framework: Which Utility When

The selection process starts with input shape classification. Object types with named properties use Pick or Omit. Union types with discrete members use Exclude or Extract. Applying union utilities to object types produces compilation errors because union operations expect string literals, not property access patterns.

interface Config {
  apiKey: string;
  timeout: number;
}

// Error: Type 'Config' does not satisfy constraint 'string | number | symbol'
type InvalidExclusion = Exclude<Config, "apiKey">;

Once the input shape category is correct, the second decision is inclusion versus exclusion. Count the properties or union members in each set. If the desired output contains fewer members than the exclusions, use the inclusive utility (Pick or Extract). If the exclusions form a shorter list, use the exclusive utility (Omit or Exclude).

The third consideration is change frequency. Types that evolve frequently benefit from inclusion-based utilities because adding a new property to the source type does not automatically add it to derived types. Exclusion-based utilities require explicit updates when new properties should be excluded.

Error messages guide correction. TypeScript reports different errors for category mismatches versus property name issues. Union utilities applied to object types produce constraint violation errors. Pick applied with nonexistent property names produces "does not exist on type" errors, while Omit accepts any string literal without complaint.

Decision factor Pick/Extract Omit/Exclude
List length Desired output is shorter than source Exclusions are shorter than output
Change frequency New properties default to excluded New properties default to included
Type safety Pick enforces property existence Omit accepts any string literal
Maintenance Explicit about included members Explicit about excluded members

The framework applies recursively to composed types. A type that uses both Pick and Partial applies each utility in sequence: first extract the desired properties, then mark them optional. The order matters because Partial operates on whatever type it receives as input.

interface FormData {
  username: string;
  email: string;
  password: string;
  confirmPassword: string;
  agreedToTerms: boolean;
}

// Extract fields, then make them optional
type PartialUpdate = Partial<Pick<FormData, "email" | "password">>;

// Equivalent to:
type PartialUpdate = {
  email?: string;
  password?: string;
};

Strict Variants and Type-Zoo Alternatives

Production TypeScript often combines standard utility types with custom mapped types to enforce stricter constraints. The type-zoo package provides battle-tested implementations of strict variants that catch common errors at compile time. Teams can implement these patterns inline or install the package as a development dependency.

OmitStrict requires that all excluded properties exist on the source type. The implementation uses a mapped type to check each key against the source type's keys before performing the exclusion.

type OmitStrict<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>;

interface User {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  passwordHash: string;
}

// Compilation error: "password" is not assignable to "id" | "email" | "passwordHash"
type InvalidOmit = OmitStrict<User, "password">;

// Compiles successfully
type ValidOmit = OmitStrict<User, "passwordHash">;

The constraint K extends keyof T forces TypeScript to verify that every property in K exists in T before allowing the type to compile. This catches typos immediately and fails compilation when refactoring renames properties without updating all Omit callsites.

PickStrict provides similar guarantees for property selection. The standard library's Pick already enforces key existence because it must access those properties to include them in the output type. The strict variant adds no additional constraint but maintains naming consistency with other strict utilities.

Union type filtering benefits from strict variants when the exclusion list might contain invalid members. ExcludeStrict enforces that all excluded members exist in the source union before performing the exclusion. The implementation requires a helper type that checks membership.

type ExcludeStrict<T, U extends T> = Exclude<T, U>;

type Status = "pending" | "approved" | "rejected";

// Compilation error: "cancelled" is not assignable to Status
type InvalidExclude = ExcludeStrict<Status, "cancelled">;

// Compiles successfully
type ValidExclude = ExcludeStrict<Status, "rejected">;

The constraint U extends T ensures that every member of the exclusion union U is also a member of the source union T. This prevents situations where exclusion lists accumulate stale values after refactoring removes union members.

Teams should adopt strict variants when the codebase meets two criteria. First, the type system must enforce correctness rather than providing flexibility for dynamic types. Second, compile-time checks must catch refactoring oversights before they reach production. Codebases that prioritize rapid prototyping over type safety may find standard utilities sufficient. For related patterns, see TypeScript Partial, Required, DeepPartial: Optional Properties That Scale.

The installation adds zero runtime overhead because all utility types disappear during compilation. The package provides TypeScript definitions only and contains no JavaScript code. Development teams can audit the implementation by reading the source code, which consists entirely of type aliases and mapped types. For a broader overview, see 10 TypeScript Utility Types That Catch Bugs Before Production.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if I use Exclude on an object type instead of a union?

TypeScript produces a compilation error stating that the type does not satisfy the constraint string | number | symbol. Exclude operates exclusively on union types and cannot remove properties from object shapes. Use Omit for object property removal.

Does Pick enforce that all specified properties exist on the source type?

Yes. Pick requires that every property name in the second type parameter exists as a key on the source type. TypeScript enforces this constraint with K extends keyof T, which means attempting to pick nonexistent properties produces a compilation error immediately.

Can Omit remove optional properties from an interface?

Yes. Omit removes any property regardless of whether it was required or optional in the source type. The operation works at the structural level and does not distinguish between required and optional properties when deciding what to exclude.

Why does OmitStrict exist when Pick already enforces key existence?

Pick enforces constraints on included properties because it must access them to construct the output type. Omit accepts any string literal as an exclusion without verification, allowing typos to compile successfully. OmitStrict adds the same constraint that Pick has natively, catching excluded property typos at compile time.

When should I use Extract instead of Pick?

Use Extract when filtering members from a union type. Use Pick when selecting properties from an object type. The operations are incompatible because unions contain discrete values while objects contain named properties. TypeScript enforces this distinction through different generic constraints on each utility.

Conclusion

TypeScript utility types operate on two distinct categories: object types with named properties and union types with discrete members. Pick and Omit transform objects. Exclude and Extract filter unions. The selection process checks input shape first, then counts members to decide between inclusion and exclusion utilities. Standard Omit accepts any string literal without verification, allowing typos and stale property names to compile successfully while producing incorrect types. Strict variants enforce property existence at compile time, trading flexibility for compile-time safety in codebases where refactoring frequency justifies the constraint. Teams that adopt this classification framework stop guessing which utility applies and start building type-safe transformations that catch errors before they reach production.

Sources

  • TypeScript: TSConfig Reference - Docs on every TSConfig option
  • TypeScript: Playground Example - Built-in Utility Types

articles.title: I Built an AI Loop That Finds "Lost My Work" Bugs and Fixes Them Until the Test Passes
articles.description: Kane CLI tests in a real browser, Codex repairs the code, and the same test runs again until it passes.
articles.body_html:
We've all done it. You fill in a long sign-up form, a job application, or a checkout, press Back or Refresh, and everything you typed is gone. These "lost my work" bugs are everywhere, and unit tests rarely catch them because they only show up in a real browser.

For the KaneCLI Online Hackathon by TestMu AI, I built StillHere: a loop that catches these bugs in a real browser and keeps fixing them until the test passes.

What it does

StillHere runs a closed loop:

  1. Find it. Kane CLI drives a real Chrome session through a journey described in plain English: fill in a checkout, open another page, press Back, press Refresh, and check the cart, details, and current step are still there.
  2. Fix it. If anything is wiped, Kane's failure report becomes a repair prompt for the Codex coding agent, which fixes the app without weakening the test.
  3. Prove it. The exact same Kane objective re-runs, unchanged, until it passes.

It works for any form or multi-step flow via --objective, not just checkout.

How I built it

Node.js with no dependencies. StillHere calls Kane CLI with --agent, parses its NDJSON result, writes a failure report with evidence and screenshots, and pipes a repair prompt to codex exec. A sample shop with a real Back/Refresh bug is included, and npm run demo:loop resets the bug so you always see fail, fix, pass. Built solo with Codex.

What Kane caught

In the recorded run, pressing "Back to checkout" wiped the order: the cart, the customer's details, and the review step were all gone. Codex fixed it by saving state in sessionStorage plus browser history and restoring it on load and Back. Kane then passed through both Back and Refresh. The test was never changed to make it pass.

Challenges

Chrome crashed when launched from a sandbox, so Kane runs from a normal terminal. Long Kane runs timed out, so the default timeout became 300 seconds. I also made sure a run with no final Kane result counts as incomplete, not as a failure for the agent to "fix."

What I learned

Verifying in a real browser catches bugs a mock never would, and keeping the test fixed is what makes an AI fix trustworthy.

What's next

A GitHub Action that runs the loop on every pull request, plus ready-made objectives for sign-up, login, and multi-step forms.

Try it

  • Code and setup: https://github.com/Mzee04/stillhere
  • Demo: https://youtu.be/4R3yvR5oKvg

What "lost my work" bugs have you run into?

articles.title: The 'Free' remove.bg Replacement Costs $144 a Year. Do the Maths First.
articles.description: Three days ago I wrote that remove.bg dies on December 1, and that the free tool on your own machine...
articles.body_html:
Three days ago I wrote that remove.bg dies on December 1, and that the free tool on your own machine could replace it. The piece did well. Then deanlee left a comment I have been thinking about ever since. He asked the question I had dodged in the original piece: at what point does paying for Canva actually cost less than paying per removal somewhere else?

I dodged it with a soft sentence. Something about the subscription maybe being the saner choice for heavy users. That is not an answer. It is a shrug dressed up as advice. So I spent this morning doing the sums properly, re-weighing the files from that first test, and recounting the pixels behind a number I now regret printing. Here is the honest version.

Problem 1: the subscription costs $144 a year, and the break-even is 12 removals a month

Canva Pro is $18 a month if you pay monthly, or $144 a year if you pay once. That works out to $12 a month. One person only. Those are the US prices, read from Canva's own pricing page in October 2026 — Canva charges different amounts in other countries, so if your pricing page shows a different currency, run the same sums with your own numbers. The background remover sits inside that paid plan, and the free plan does not have it.

Now the other side. After December 1, the thing you compare it against is not remove.bg's $9 subscription. That plan stops existing. The honest comparison is paying per image, and remove.bg's smallest one-off pack is $3 for 3 credits. One credit takes the background out of one photo. That is $1 a removal.

Twelve dollars divided by one dollar is twelve. If you pay Canva yearly, you need to remove 12 backgrounds a month before the subscription beats paying a dollar a time. Pay monthly instead, and the line moves to 18 a month.

Bigger packs bend the number. The $49 pack works out to 65 cents a removal, and against that Canva only wins past 19 removals a month on yearly billing, 28 on monthly. The $199 pack drops it to 40 cents, and then you need 30 a month yearly, 45 monthly. So the real answer is a range, not a single number: somewhere between 12 and 30 a month, depending on how you buy the one-off credits.

And one more honest wrinkle. If you already pay for Canva because you use its templates or its brand tools, the remover costs you nothing extra. Your break-even is zero. This maths only bites if background removal is the thing pushing you to pay in the first place.

One gap I could not close: several reviews this year say Canva's paid AI tools share a monthly allowance, and I could not confirm whether the background remover draws from it. If you cut out hundreds of photos a month, look at the limit on your own plan before you assume it is bottomless.

Problem 2: the cheap price you remember is a ghost

This is the part that changes the answer most. In my first piece I quoted remove.bg's $9 plan, 40 images, about 23 cents each. That number is real, and it is also dead in two weeks. Subscriptions end on December 1 and unused one-off credits expire the same day. Comparing Canva against 23 cents is comparing against a price nobody will be able to pay after the shutdown.

The fair comparison is what you can actually buy on December 2: a dollar a removal at the small end. That is the number the break-even above uses.

If you still hold remove.bg credits, use them before December 1. After that they are gone, and so is the argument that paid removal costs 23 cents.

Problem 3: the PNG weighs more than I told you

In the first piece I said the shoe went in as a 128 KB JPEG and came out as a 632 KB PNG, and I waved at compression as the fix. I should have weighed it properly then. I have now, using the same cut-outs from that morning.

Same shoe, same pixels, three formats. The PNG is 632 KB. Saved as WebP with the transparency kept, at a quality setting where I could not spot a difference at normal viewing size, it is 94 KB. That is 6.75 times smaller. Flattened onto white and saved as a JPEG, it is 99 KB, or 6.37 times smaller. The portrait is worse: a 1.56 MB PNG becomes a 192 KB WebP, 8.13 times smaller, or a 234 KB JPEG, 6.69 times smaller.

So the "five times" figure floating around my draft notes was wrong in the generous direction. It is six to eight times on real photos with a real subject. The one exception was the mountain lake photo, where the PNG was only 3.5 times the WebP, because there was almost nothing in the file to compress in the first place.

I also built a small test page with one shoe on it, in all three formats, and measured what actually travels down the wire. The PNG page moves 632 KB. The WebP page moves 94 KB. Scale that to a shop with 40 product shots and the PNG version ships 24.7 MB of images where the WebP version ships 3.7 MB. That is the difference between a page that opens and a page your customer stares at.

The fix costs nothing. Convert the cut-out to WebP before it goes on a page, and keep the PNG only as your master copy. Lossless WebP barely helps, about 1.4 times smaller, so it has to be the lossy setting to matter.

Problem 4: the 71.7% number was right, and it meant nothing

This is the one I owe readers a correction on. In the first piece I printed "71.7% transparent" for the mountain lake photo, then said in the next paragraph that the number meant nothing because the remaining 28% was a grey blob. Both halves were true, and printing the number at all was still a mistake, because a table makes any number look measured.

I recounted it pixel by pixel from the actual file. 689,221 of 961,200 pixels are fully transparent. That is 71.70%. The number was correct. The shoe was 73.48% against the 73.5% I printed, and the portrait 66.78% against 66.8%. All three check out.

But here is what the recount found that the table hid. In the lake photo, only 7 pixels in the entire image are fully solid. Seven. The other 28.3% of the picture is made of half-transparent pixels, a thin wash of grey where the tool could not decide what was subject and what was sky. A transparency percentage counts pixels. It cannot tell you whether the pixels it kept form a shoe or a smudge. No percentage can. Only looking at the picture can, and when I looked, the picture was a ghost.

The recount also explains the file sizes above. Even the good cut-outs are mostly half-transparent edge pixels, 24% of the shoe and 32% of the portrait. Soft edges are why the tool looks good, and soft edges are exactly what makes a PNG balloon.

What I would actually do

If you remove backgrounds a few times a month, do not buy a subscription for it. Pay a dollar when you need one, or run the free tool on your own machine and spend eight seconds a photo instead. Twelve removals a month is the line, and most people never cross it.

If you cross it every month, and you do it inside Canva already, pay yearly and stop thinking about it. The $144 works out to $12 a month, and the per-removal price stops mattering.

And whatever you switch to, do not ship the PNG. Convert it. The cut-out is free. The page weight is the bill you pay later, every time someone opens your site.

Now I want the other side of this. How many backgrounds do you actually remove in a month, the real count, not the guess? And if you already switched away from remove.bg, what did you switch to, and what did it cost once you counted everything? If enough of you answer with real numbers, I will run the same maths on your answers and print the correction if I got any of this wrong.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: I built shadcn/ui for Angular 22: install it or own the source
articles.description: Ivorie: 54 Angular components with the shadcn/ui look. Signals, zoneless, SSR, Tailwind 4. An npm package, or a CLI that copies the code into your app.
articles.body_html:
React developers have had shadcn/ui for a while: good-looking components, accessible by default, and code you own. I work in Angular, and I wanted the same thing for Angular. Same classes, same variants, same feel, and current Angular, not something ported from an older version.

I couldn't find a close match, so I built it. It's called Ivorie, it's MIT, and version 1.5.2 is on npm today.

This post shows what it does with real code you can paste.

  • Repo: https://github.com/Inlaylab/ivorie
  • Docs and playground: https://inlaylab.github.io/ivorie/

Ivorie is an independent project. It's not affiliated with shadcn/ui. It ports shadcn/ui's design (MIT) to Angular, with credit.

What you get

  • 54 components with the shadcn/ui look and behavior. Keyboard and ARIA follow Radix patterns.
  • Angular 22 only. Signal inputs, model(), zoneless, SSR. It also works in NgModule apps.
  • Tailwind CSS 4.
  • Two ways in. Install @inlaylab/ivorie from npm and get updates. Or run the ivorie CLI, which copies the source into your app so you can edit it.
  • 13 styles (shadcn's eight plus glass, bento, mono, graphite and tint), 7 base colors, 17 accent colors, 26 fonts, 5 radius options.
  • 5 icon libraries: Lucide, Tabler, Phosphor, Hugeicons, Remix.
  • A data table with sort, pagination, filter, selection and column visibility. It runs in the browser or against your API.
  • 22 blocks: login, sign-up, sidebar and dashboard pages, already wired.

Path 1: the npm package 

npm i @inlaylab/ivorie @angular/cdk @lucide/angular
npm i -D tailwindcss @tailwindcss/postcss tw-animate-css

/* src/styles.css */
@import "@inlaylab/ivorie/styles/theme.css";
@import "@inlaylab/ivorie/styles/style-nova.css";

Add class="style-nova" to <body>. Then import only what you use. Each component has its own entry point, so your bundle carries only those:

import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { IvButton } from '@inlaylab/ivorie/button';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  imports: [IvButton],
  template: `<button ivButton>Save</button>`,
})
export class App {}

The full setup, with the Tailwind config, is on the Installation page.

Path 2: copy the source and own it

This is the shadcn way. The code lands in your repo. Change anything.

npx ivorie init
npx ivorie add button dialog

init sets up the theme, the style and components.json. add copies components to src/app/ui by default (--path changes that). You can even pick your own selector prefix with --prefix.

Both paths come from one source. The CLI copies from the same library code that npm ships, so they don't drift apart.

A sortable table in 30 lines

The data table isn't one big component. It's five small features: ivSort, ivFilter, ivPagination, ivRowSelection and ivColumnVisibility. Rows go in and rows come out, as signals. Use one, or all five. The cells stay in your template.

Here's sorting on its own:

import { ChangeDetectionStrategy, Component, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { IV_DATA_TABLE_IMPORTS, IvColumnDef, ivSort } from '@inlaylab/ivorie/data-table';

interface Release { version: string; name: string; }

const RELEASES: Release[] = [
  { version: '1.2.0', name: 'Playground' },
  { version: '1.10.0', name: 'Later work' },
  { version: '1.0.0', name: 'First release' },
];

const COLUMNS: IvColumnDef<Release>[] = [
  { id: 'version', header: 'Version', accessor: (r) => r.version, sortable: true },
  { id: 'name', header: 'Name', accessor: (r) => r.name, sortable: true },
];

@Component({
  selector: 'app-releases',
  imports: [IV_DATA_TABLE_IMPORTS],
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
  template: `
    <iv-table class="rounded-lg border">
      <thead ivTableHeader>
        <tr ivTableRow>
          @for (c of columns; track c.id) {
            <th [ivDataTableSort]="c.id" [sort]="sort">{{ c.header }}</th>
          }
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody ivTableBody>
        @for (r of sort.rows(); track r.version) {
          <tr ivTableRow>
            <td ivTableCell class="font-mono">{{ r.version }}</td>
            <td ivTableCell>{{ r.name }}</td>
          </tr>
        }
      </tbody>
    </iv-table>
  `,
})
export class Releases {
  protected readonly columns = COLUMNS;
  protected readonly sort = ivSort(signal(RELEASES), {
    columns: COLUMNS,
    initial: { id: 'version', desc: false },
  });
}

The sort header sets aria-sort and works with the keyboard. Versions sort as numbers, so 1.10.0 comes after 1.2.0.

Server mode

When the data lives on your server, switch to mode: 'server'. The table stops sorting and paging in the browser. Instead it gives you one query() signal with the page, sort and filter. Feed that to resource() or httpResource():

protected readonly table: IvDataTable<Order> = ivDataTable<Order>({
  mode: 'server',
  data: computed(() => this.page().rows),
  rowCount: computed(() => this.page().total),
  columns: COLUMNS,
  getRowId: (o) => String(o.id),
  pageSize: 5,
});

protected readonly orders = resource<OrderPage, IvDataTableQuery>({
  params: () => this.table.query(),
  loader: ({ params, abortSignal }) => fetchOrders(params, abortSignal),
});

It's the same API in both modes. The full example, with the loading and empty rows, is on the data table page.

A login page in one command

Blocks are whole pages. They're wired, not just markup: reactive forms with validation, typed outputs, and pending and error inputs.

npx ivorie add login-01

This writes the page to src/app/blocks/login-01/. It also adds the components the page needs, fixes the imports, and renames the icons to your icon library. All that's left is your auth call:

@Component({
  selector: 'app-login-01',
  imports: [LoginForm],
  template: `
    <div class="w-full max-w-sm">
      <app-login-01-form (submitted)="login($event)" (provider)="loginWith($event)" />
    </div>
  `,
})
export class Login01 {
  protected login(value: LoginValue): void {
    // Call your auth API here, then navigate.
  }

  protected loginWith(provider: 'google' | 'github' | 'apple'): void {
    // Start your OAuth flow here.
  }
}

There are 22 blocks: five logins, five sign-ups, eight sidebars and four dashboards. See them live at /blocks.

Make it look like your product

Open the playground. Pick a style, base color, font, heading font, radius and icon library. Real components update as you click. Then copy one command:

# new app
npx ivorie init --preset ivp1_…

# existing app: change the whole look
npx ivorie apply ivp1_…

The ivp1_… code holds your whole look, so you can share it with your team or paste it in an issue. Flags work too:

npx ivorie init --style glass --base-color zinc --radius large --icon-library tabler

Changing icon libraries later? npx ivorie migrate icons --from lucide --to tabler renames the icons in your own templates as well.

A note on the new styles: glass uses backdrop-filter. Where that isn't supported, or the user asks for reduced transparency, it turns solid. Every style has a test that checks text contrast (4.5:1 or more) for every base color, in light and dark mode.

How it's built

A few choices you may care about:

  • Signals all the way down. input(), model(), output(), computed(). No @Input() decorators. A lint rule blocks them.
  • No @angular/animations. Motion is CSS through tw-animate-css.
  • SSR is tested on every change. The docs app is server-rendered, and a smoke test loads every page in a real browser.
  • One command for every gate. npm run check runs every build, the unit specs (Vitest, with axe for accessibility), SSR, the package and CLI tests, and the lint rules.
  • The registry uses the shadcn registry JSON format.
  • Releases carry npm provenance and are published from GitHub Actions.

What's next, and how you can help

  • 1.6: more theme dials: density, and how much glass.
  • 1.7: AI-ready. An AGENTS.md that ivorie init writes, llms.txt for the docs, and an MCP server so coding agents can browse and add components.

I'd love help with these, and with the smaller issues labeled good first issue. There are new blocks to build, CLI commands like ivorie list and ivorie diff, and docs search. Read CONTRIBUTING.md, run npm install && npm run check, and you're set.

If you try it, tell me what broke or what you missed. Issues are the most useful thing you can give a new library. If it saves you time, a star on GitHub helps other Angular devs find it.

Thanks for reading.

articles.title: Show DEV: Monetizing an Open Source WebRTC App Without Stripe, Subscriptions, or Paywalls (Part 2)
articles.description: How I built an on-chain, zero-trust micropayment and licensing engine with USDC on Base and Polygon—keeping P2P free forever while selling TURN relay passes and enterprise white-labeling.
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

🚀 Live Web App (Free, No Signup): air-stream.pages.dev

⭐ GitHub Repo (MIT): github.com/QuantumTechCoder/AirStream

📖 Missed Part 1? Catch up here: Show DEV: AirStream — Stream Gigabytes Browser-to-Browser with WebRTC (No Cloud, No Size Limits)

The Indie Hacker's Worst Dilemma

In Part 1 of this series, I shared how I built AirStream—an open-source PWA that opens encrypted, direct browser-to-browser data tunnels using WebRTC RTCDataChannel, letting people stream 10GB+ files at gigabit Wi-Fi speeds without cloud servers or size caps.

The feedback was incredible. But within 48 hours of launching, I hit the universal wall that every open-source builder eventually crashes into:

  1. Bandwidth isn't 100% free when firewalls get aggressive. Standard STUN traversal handles ~85–90% of home networks. But users on strict corporate firewalls, university Wi-Fi, and symmetric mobile cellular NATs (like Reliance Jio or AT&T) require TURN relay fallback servers. High-bandwidth TURN relays cost real money to maintain.
  2. I despise aggressive SaaS paywalls. Slapping a 2GB cap, forcing user registrations, or putting intrusive Google Ad banners on a clean privacy-first tool destroys everything that makes open-source great.
  3. Traditional payment processors (Stripe, PayPal) are terrible for lightweight indie apps.

So I asked myself: How can I keep AirStream 100% free and open-source forever, while creating ethical, frictionless revenue streams that actually respect user privacy?

Here is the story of how I designed an on-chain, zero-trust micropayment architecture powered by USDC on Base and Polygon—and why web3 stablecoins turned out to be the ultimate indie monetization rail.

Why Traditional Payment Rails Failed

When considering payments for an open-source tool, traditional options like Stripe or Lemonsqueezy seem like the default choice. But for AirStream, they created massive architectural friction:

  • 💸 The Flat-Fee Trap: Stripe charges roughly \$0.30 + 2.9% per transaction. If someone transfers a 30GB video file and wants to send a \$1 or \$2 tip to say "thanks for saving my evening," 35% to 40% of their tip gets vaporized by processing fees.
  • 🌐 Global Friction & KYC Walls: A huge portion of our users are developers, video editors, and students in India, Latin America, Southeast Asia, and Eastern Europe. Stripe Checkout often rejects international cards or requires phone numbers, postal codes, and 3D-Secure redirects.
  • 🗄️ Database & Auth Bloat: To verify paid subscriptions with Stripe Webhooks, I would have had to spin up a PostgreSQL database, write authentication logic (JWTs / OAuth), and store user emails. AirStream has zero logins, zero databases, and zero user telemetry. Introducing accounts just to process payments felt backwards.

The Architecture: Zero-Trust On-Chain USDC (Base & Polygon)

Instead of traditional merchant processors, I implemented native USDC payments on Layer-2 networks (Base and Polygon).

Why Base and Polygon?

  1. Negligible Gas Fees: Transferring USDC on Base or Polygon costs under \$0.01 (often \$0.003–\$0.005).
  2. Stable Currency: USDC is pegged 1:1 to the US Dollar—no crypto price volatility for either the user or the developer.
  3. Decentralized Verification: No backend database needed. The blockchain is an immutable public ledger. The client app can verify payments directly against decentralized RPC nodes!

Maximum Security: Preventing Spoofed Payments

One of the biggest requirements was: Make sure no one can fake payments or forge transactions.

In a client-side web application, you cannot just trust a frontend input box that says "I paid! Here's a transaction hash." An attacker could try to:

  • Paste a random transaction hash from an unrelated transfer.
  • Paste a failed or reverted transaction.
  • Paste a real transaction sent to someone else's wallet.
  • Send 0.000001 USDC and claim a 30 USDC license.
  • Reuse an old transaction hash from another user.

To make the verification 100% zero-trust, I engineered an on-chain validator in TypeScript that inspects the raw EVM transaction receipts via decentralized JSON-RPC nodes:

// src/utils/paymentVerifier.ts
export async function verifyOnChainPayment(
  txHash: string,
  expectedChain: SupportedChain,
  minUsdcAmount: number
): Promise<VerificationResult> {
  const cleanHash = txHash.trim();

  // 1. Verify 64-character hex format
  if (!/^0x([A-Fa-f0-9]{64})$/.test(cleanHash)) {
    return { valid: false, error: 'Invalid transaction hash format.' };
  }

  // 2. Fetch immutable transaction receipt directly from RPC
  const receipt = await rpcCall(expectedChain, 'eth_getTransactionReceipt', [cleanHash]);
  if (!receipt) {
    return { valid: false, error: 'Transaction still pending in mempool.' };
  }

  // 3. Ensure the transaction actually succeeded (status 0x1)
  if (receipt.status !== '0x1') {
    return { valid: false, error: 'Transaction was reverted on-chain.' };
  }

  const recipientNormalized = RECIPIENT_WALLET.toLowerCase();
  const network = NETWORKS[expectedChain];
  let isMatched = false;
  let matchedUsdcAmount = 0;

  // 4. Parse raw EVM event logs for ERC-20 Transfer
  if (Array.isArray(receipt.logs)) {
    for (const log of receipt.logs) {
      const contract = (log.address || '').toLowerCase();
      const isUsdc = contract === network.usdcAddress.toLowerCase();

      // Topic 0: Transfer(address,address,uint256) signature
      if (isUsdc && log.topics && log.topics[0] === TRANSFER_TOPIC) {
        // Topic 2: Recipient address (padded to 32 bytes)
        const toAddress = '0x' + log.topics[2].slice(26).toLowerCase();

        if (toAddress === recipientNormalized) {
          const rawValue = BigInt(log.data);
          const actualAmount = Number(rawValue) / Math.pow(10, network.usdcDecimals);

          // Verify exact expected amount (with 1% micro-rounding tolerance)
          if (actualAmount >= minUsdcAmount * 0.99) {
            matchedUsdcAmount = actualAmount;
            isMatched = true;
            break;
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }

  if (!isMatched) {
    return { valid: false, error: 'No matching USDC payment found in this receipt.' };
  }

  return { valid: true, txHash: cleanHash, amount: matchedUsdcAmount };
}

How this guarantees cryptographic security:

  • Receipt Status: If a transaction reverted or threw an out-of-gas error, receipt.status !== '0x1' rejects it.
  • Contract Address Matching: Only official USDC contract addresses (0x833589... on Base, 0x3c499c... on Polygon) are parsed. Custom fake ERC-20 tokens are ignored.
  • Topic Decoding: Decodes the padded 32-byte to address to ensure funds actually arrived at developer address 0x2cef0473f985156eDe84312Ce0BeB94B602d26E4.
  • Decimal Precision: Computes the exact integer value divided by $10^6$ (USDC decimals) to ensure the full amount was paid.

The Sustainable Monetization Pillars

With zero-trust on-chain verification in place, I introduced two practical commercial offerings that keep the core P2P app 100% free while funding ongoing relay infrastructure:

1. Firewall-Bypass TURN Relay Pro Pass (3 USDC / 3 Months)

For 90% of transfers, direct STUN works out of the box and is 100% free forever.

However, students behind university firewalls or colleagues in strict corporate networks with symmetric NATs cannot establish direct UDP hole-punches.

  • Pricing: 3 USDC for 3 months (just \$1/month).
  • Benefits:
    • Direct access to high-bandwidth TCP/TLS TURN relays over port 443 (which corporate firewalls cannot block).
    • Custom enterprise TURN server inputs: Users can plug in their own private coturn or Twilio TURN credentials directly into the client.
  • Client-Side Storage: The verified license and expiration timestamp are saved locally in localStorage, meaning zero accounts and zero tracked user data.

2. Custom White-Label Deployment for Teams & Agencies (30 USDC)

Video production agencies, law firms, and medical clinics frequently deal with sensitive multi-gigabyte files. They don't want their clients to see an AirStream logo, nor do they want to pay \$20–\$30/user/month to WeTransfer or Dropbox Teams.

For a one-time setup fee of 30 USDC:

  • Deployment on their custom domain (e.g. transfer.agency.com).
  • Custom branding, company logo, color palette, and favicon.
  • Dedicated private TURN relay with unthrottled bandwidth.
  • Full source code ownership & 24-hour turnaround.

What I Learned: Web3 as the Indie Hacker's Payment Rail
