articles.title: Could I Still Do This From Scratch?
articles.description: The thing that every dev I know is quietly worrying about is not AI taking their job. It's losing the...
articles.body_html:
The thing that every dev I know is quietly worrying about is not AI taking their job. It's losing the skill to do their job.

We're not talking about it out loud because it feels like admitting weakness, and because these tools are genuinely powerful. You can roll out a feature in an afternoon that previously took you a week. Autocomplete guesses what you're thinking. A chat agent lets you restructure that flaky module you've been avoiding for months. But then in that in-between moment, the third or fourth prompt, the third or fourth tab-tab-tab-accept cycle, that quiet question pops up: could I still do this from scratch?

Now don't get me wrong, I'm not saying that devs couldn't write a for loop if they wanted to. I'm saying that this part is what's fading. The deep work of wrestling with a problem, thinking it through, fumbling around in the dark until the solution crystallizes. Because instead of spending fifteen minutes thinking through the problem, the model gives you the answer in fifteen seconds, so what you're doing is no longer building something. You're reviewing it, which is a far less taxing and less creative task.

The research is starting to catch up with this concern. In a Microsoft study presented at CHI 2025, 319 knowledge workers showed a clear trend: the higher the trust in AI-generated content, the lower the level of critical thinking. The change in workflow is not about problem solving, but about checking and integrating. In another study, this time from MIT Media Lab about essay writing, people who used LLMs were the ones with the worst brain connectivity. They called it cognitive debt. Even productivity is more doubtful than the hype says: in a 2025 study by METR, experienced open source developers using AI tools turned out to be slower than those who didn't, but convinced themselves of the opposite.

All the devs I know have felt this, not as some abstract fear, but as a concrete experience of reaching for an answer and realizing the shelf is empty. I don't need a study to tell me that the knowledge I used to have is slipping away. That the syntax I once produced on autopilot is now a few keystrokes and a prompt away. That the kind of instinct only a developer who's been through dozens of bad architectural decisions can have is now being outsourced to a model that has seen a million architectures but never lived inside one.

The scary part is that it happens under the radar. You're still writing good code, because the model writes good code. You're still getting good performance reviews. You're still shipping. Until you're not, and that's when the tools don't work: when a weird bug shows up, when a novel constraint hits, when an edge case the training data never saw appears. Only then do you realize if there's actually a developer under the hood, or if it's just a workflow.

No one wants to go back to the old days of writing boilerplate the hard way. But the devs who are quietly preparing are doing it in the not-so-cool way: writing some code without AI, wrestling through the confusion, keeping those weak muscles working. The scary part is not that AI will replace you. It's that one day you'll wake up and you'll have replaced yourself, one accepted suggestion at a time.

articles.title: Part 6: The Walkthrough That Only Worked on My Machine
articles.description: This is Part 6 of a series building an HL7 v2-to-FHIR R4 interoperability service in public. The...
articles.body_html:
This is Part 6 of a series building an HL7 v2-to-FHIR R4 interoperability service in public. The repository is ND-codes/nhs-interop-platform,
and the code as it stood for this article is tagged part-6.

This week's plan was a ten-minute tour of the repository and the questions an interviewer asks about it. Before writing the tour, I did the obvious thing and followed the one I already had.

It doesn't work on a machine that isn't mine. Not in a subtle way.

A walkthrough is a promise

Most of what a repository claims is hard to check. A threat model, an
architecture diagram, a note about scaling: a reader takes those on trust or not at all.

A quickstart is different. It is a sequence of commands with stated outcomes, and the reader finds out within minutes whether you were telling the truth. It is the most falsifiable document in the repository and usually the least tested, because the author is the one person who can never run it fresh.

Mine had four failures. Three of them break on the reader's machine and work perfectly on mine. The fourth was not about machines at all.

make test could not run outside Git Bash

Step 7 of my quickstart said make test. The recipe:

docker run --rm -v "$$(cygpath -m $$(cd services/$$svc && pwd))":/app -w //app python:3.12-slim \
  sh -c "pip install -q -r requirements-dev.txt && pytest -q"

cygpath converts a Windows path into the C:/ form Docker wants. It exists
in Git Bash on Windows and nowhere else. On macOS or Linux that line is
cygpath: command not found, and make test and make lint both die on the
first service.

I work in Git Bash on Windows. It had never once failed for me, which is the entire problem.

The fix keeps the Windows behaviour exactly and adds the other path:

abs=$(cd services/$svc && pwd) ; wd=/app ;
if command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1 ; then abs=$(cygpath -m "$abs") ; wd=//app ; fi ;
docker run --rm -v "$abs":/app -w "$wd" python:3.12-slim ...

The doubled //app is the other half of the same problem. MSYS rewrites a leading /app into a Windows path, so Git Bash needs it doubled and nothing else does. Both branches were tested, the second by putting a fake cygpath on PATH. Then the Git Bash branch ran for real on my machine: 92 tests, all
passing.

make integration installed into the system interpreter 

python3 -m pip install --quiet httpx pytest

On Debian, Ubuntu and Homebrew Python 3.11 and later, that is refused outright. PEP 668 lets a distribution mark its base interpreter as externally managed, and pip then declines with error: externally-managed-environment. It works on my machine because my Python is not marked that way.

It builds a throwaway virtualenv now, with a bin and Scripts fallback so the same line works in Git Bash.

A file the quickstart told you to copy did not exist 

cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars

There was no terraform.tfvars.example. There never had been. You only find that by following your own instructions as though you had not written them.

The alert that reached nobody

The fourth is the one worth the article, and I did not find it. Nan, a reader of Part 4, did.

Part 4 was about an alert that could never fire, because it watched a metric no service exported. I fixed that, exported the gauge, wrote the rule unit tests, added the runbook sections, and built scripts to open the circuit breaker on purpose so you could watch PDSCircuitOpen go Firing.

Nan's question was roughly: and then who gets told?

Nobody. Here is the whole chain:

  • observability/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml exists, and is a reasonable config. It routes by severity, groups by alertname and service, and has an inhibit rule.
  • Nothing starts an Alertmanager. There is no such service in Docker Compose and no such manifest anywhere in k8s/.
  • prometheus.yml had no alerting block, so even if one had been running, Prometheus did not know where it was.
  • That config's smtp_smarthost pointed at mailhog:1025. No file in the repository has ever started a mailhog.

So the rules evaluated, turned red in the Prometheus UI, and stopped there.
Meanwhile docs/architecture.md said "Alertmanager routes pages" and the runbook's prerequisites told the on-call engineer they would need access to "the alerts Slack/PagerDuty queue".

Part 4 made the alert fireable. Part 5 made the documentation honest about the controls. Neither of us noticed that the last hop did not exist, and it is the hop that makes the other two matter. An alert nobody receives is a dashboard.

The fix is small, which is the irritating part:

alerting:
  alertmanagers:
    - static_configs:
        - targets: ['alertmanager:9093']

Plus two services in Compose. Alertmanager and Mailpit as the destination: a disposable SMTP sink with a web inbox, which holds mail in memory and forwards it nowhere. That is what makes it safe to point a demo at. I used Mailpit rather than the MailHog the old config named, because MailHog has not been released since 2020 and Part 5 was about not shipping things you would not defend.

Now make break-pds opens the breaker, PDSCircuitOpen goes Firing about two minutes later, and the notification arrives at a web inbox on port 8025 where you can read it. The whole path, end to end, is a demo you can run on a laptop.

I ran it on 17 November, and again this morning for the screenshots. The subject line began [FIRING:1] PDSCircuitOpen transform. Six parts in, it is the first alert this project has ever delivered to anything.

The inbox also holds two IngestNoTraffic alerts I did not ask for. I checked the rule in alerts.yml before calling it a fault: it fires once ingest has gone 15 minutes without an HL7 message, and the stack sat idle overnight. So it is expected, but a demo stack left running will email you about its own quiet.

Making the tour testable

The underlying failure is that a quickstart is prose, and prose does not run in CI. So the tour is now a script, and make walkthrough runs it.

Eight checks. The stack is up, ingest accepts an ADT, the Patient reaches FHIR keyed on the NHS number, a lab result produces Observations, Prometheus is scraping every service, Prometheus has discovered an Alertmanager, Alertmanager is healthy, and the inbox is reachable. Each one fails loudly and stops.

The sixth is the one that would have caught Nan's finding:

discovered=$(curl -sf "$PROM/api/v1/alertmanagers" \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(len(json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]["activeAlertmanagers"]))')
[ "$discovered" -ge 1 ] || fail "Prometheus has no active Alertmanager."

Two small things I would do again. The FHIR checks parse the Bundle rather than grepping for "total", because the whitespace is not guaranteed and a grep for that string also matches a zero. And the Mailpit check asserts reachability but reads the message count defensively, because I could not get Mailpit's API documentation to load and I was not willing to assert a field name I had not seen. A schema change should not turn a working inbox into a failed tour.

The tour failed its own first run

The script was written and checked without a Docker daemon. The first time it ran against a real stack, it stopped at check 3:

[3/8] The Patient reaches FHIR, keyed on the NHS number
      FAIL the Patient did not become true within 30s

The Patient was there. Asking HAPI for a count returned one. The query was the problem. A FHIR token search separates system and code with a pipe,
identifier=https://fhir.nhs.uk/Id/nhs-number|9000000009, and RFC 3986 does
not allow an unencoded | in a query string. HAPI runs on Tomcat, which enforces that by default and answers HTTP 400.

The 400 never reached the screen. curl -sf turns any HTTP error into a silent non-zero exit, and the retry loop read that as "not there yet". Thirty seconds later it reported a missing Patient that was never missing.

The fix is %7C in place of the pipe, in the script and in the quickstart. The quickstart needed it too: Tomcat's own documentation says the major browsers send that character unencoded, so the link would have failed in a browser as well.

This is the alert story again, at a smaller scale. A check that cannot tell "not found" from "you asked the wrong way" will pass or fail for the wrong reason, and you only find out by running it.

Four things the architecture document still claimed

While I was at it. docs/architecture.md said messages are dead-lettered to S3, which Part 5 established is false. It said GitLab CI gates quality, two weeks after we deleted .gitlab-ci.yml. It said CI pushes to an image registry, which it does not, because there is nowhere to push to. And it said "every request is traced", when what actually exists is a trace id carried in log lines. That is correlation, not distributed tracing, and there is no OpenTelemetry in any of these services.

All four are corrected in place, with a short note saying what each one used to claim. Quietly editing them would have been tidier and worse.

The questions an interviewer actually asks

This is the other half of what Part 6 was meant to cover, and the walkthrough work made it easier rather than harder, because the questions people ask about a system are mostly the ones a broken walkthrough exposes.

Walk me through what happens to a message.

It arrives at POST /hl7 on ingest, which validates the MSH segment and assigns a trace id. Transform parses it, maps it to a FHIR R4 transaction Bundle, optionally enriches the Patient from PDS, and writes the Bundle to HAPI FHIR with a conditional update keyed on the NHS number. Failures dead-letter to a local path. The trace id
follows the message through all three services.

What happens when PDS is down?

Enrichment fails open. A circuit breaker
opens after five consecutive failures, and the pipeline keeps writing Patients with locally derived demographics. Data quality degrades; no clinical message is dropped. That is a deliberate trade-off and it is the seventh Caldicott principle in practice, the one that says the duty to share can matter as much as the duty to protect. You can watch it with make break-pds.

Who gets paged?

Until this week, nobody, and I would say exactly that. The
rules evaluated and notified no one. It is fixed for the local stack and still missing in Kubernetes. A question like this is a gift, because the honest answer is more interesting than the tidy one.

How do you know the mapping is correct?

Unit tests per defect, each written to fail against the previous code. Part 3 covers nine specific ways an HL7 v2 to FHIR mapping goes wrong, most of them found by readers. The honest limit is that there is no conformance suite and no validation against the HL7 v2 to FHIR
implementation guide; the tests encode the defects we know about.

Where does patient data live and for how long?

Mapped fields in HAPI FHIR on Postgres. Complete raw messages in the dead-letter path, which holds more patient data than the FHIR store does, for up to 72 hours. That retention is new as of Part 5 and the path still does not survive a pod restart.

What is the worst bug you have shipped here?

Part 4's fix for the alert that could never fire. The circuit breaker was applied as a decorator to a coroutine function, so it counted the returned coroutine object as a success and never opened, which means the gauge I had just added and the alert I had just made fireable still could not fire. The test passed because it drove the breaker synchronously. I found it by running the stack.

How would you scale it?

The ingest-to-transform hop is synchronous HTTP,
which keeps the local demo one command and is the first thing I would replace with an SQS FIFO queue using the NHS number as the message group id so a patient's messages stay ordered. Beyond that the services are stateless and scale horizontally; the bottleneck is the FHIR write path.

What would you do differently?

Wrote the documentation last. Almost every false claim in this repository was true of the design at the moment it was
written and never revisited.

What I did not fix

There is still no Alertmanager in the Helm charts, so the Kubernetes path notifies nobody. I did not write one, because I cannot deploy a cluster to test it and shipping untested YAML two days before publishing is the exact thing Part 5 was about. It is in the "Claimed, not built" section of docs/security.md and a roadmap issue.

There is no paging integration anywhere. The Alertmanager config has a PagerDuty receiver commented out and has never been pointed at a routing key.

make restore-pds brings PDS back but does not clear the alert. The breaker only tries the call again when the next request arrives, so with no traffic it stays open and PDSCircuitOpen keeps firing after the outage is over. One synthetic message closed it. The restore script should send that message, and the runbook should say so. That is next week's pull request.

The retry loop still hides the status code. The pipe is fixed, but the next malformed query would fail the same silent way.

And I have not timed the tour on a second machine. The series plan called this part a ten-minute walkthrough; the document now says the figure should be yours rather than mine.

Worth stealing

Run your own quickstart on a machine you did not configure. A colleague's, a fresh VM, a container. The author is the one person who cannot test it.

Grep your build tooling for anything platform-specific. cygpath, open, sed -i with a bare -i, realpath, date -d. Each one quietly scopes your repository to one operating system.

Make the tour a target. Prose cannot run in CI; a script can, and then the document and the repository cannot drift apart silently.

Check the last hop of anything that is supposed to tell a human. Working alert rules that notify nobody look identical to working alerting from inside the repository.

Correct a stale claim in place, with a line saying what it used to say. The
edit history is not where a reader looks.

Where AI helps here, and where it doesn't

I built this with Claude Code, and this week drew the line unusually clearly.

Reading the Makefile and noticing that cygpath is Git Bash only is exactly the kind of thing it is good at. So is knowing that PEP 668 would refuse the pip line, and checking terraform.tfvars.example against the variables that are actually declared. That sweep took minutes, and I would not have done it by hand two days before publishing.

But none of that is the same as running the thing. It wrote and checked this week's changes in a sandbox with no Docker daemon, so "works on my machine" problems were invisible to it by construction. It found the cygpath problem by reading, after I pointed it at the walkthrough, which is not the same as the problem announcing itself.

The walkthrough script is the clearest example. It was reviewed, shellchecked and clean, and it failed its first real run on a URL encoding rule. Once the stack was up on my machine, the same assistant ran the query directly, found the 400 in about a minute, and checked the fix against the RFC and Tomcat's documentation. Reading wrote the bug. Running found it.

The alert delivery gap is the sharper case. It was not found by reading at all, by a model or by me. Nan found it by asking the one question neither of us had: and then who gets told? Two articles in a row went past it while looking directly at the alerting configuration.

The pattern I would now state plainly, three weeks running: reading finds inconsistencies, running finds defects, and other people find the questions.

Sources

  • PEP 668, on externally managed Python environments
  • Prometheus configuration, for the top-level alerting block
  • Prometheus HTTP API, for the /api/v1/alertmanagers response shape
  • RFC 3986, section 3.4, the characters allowed in a URI query
  • Apache Tomcat HTTP connector, relaxedQueryChars and the characters rejected by default
  • Mailpit, Docker install
  • The Caldicott Principles, National Data Guardian
  • Alertmanager and Prometheus configurations in this article were validated with amtool check-config 0.34.1 and promtool check config

Next

Part 7 is the last one: where AI fits in this work and where it does not, with seven weeks of specifics rather than opinions.

If you have a quickstart in a repository you maintain, run it somewhere else this week. What broke first?

This is a personal project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NHS England or any NHS organisation. It uses the public PDS FHIR sandbox and synthetic test data only. Views are my own.

articles.title: Git 2.56's git add --resolved only checks conflict markers while git still calls a file unmerged
articles.description: I tested Git 2.56's new add --resolved flag: it kept an unrelated edit out of a merge commit, but its conflict-marker check stopped working the moment the index stopped calling a file unmerged.
articles.body_html:
Git 2.56 shipped a new flag for the oldest bad habit in merge conflict resolution: typing git add . the moment the markers are gone, and staging whatever else happened to be sitting in the working tree at the same time.

git add --resolved is supposed to fix that. It stages only the paths git still considers unmerged, and it is meant to refuse if any of those paths still contain leftover conflict markers. I built it from source, because the Ubuntu 24.04 container I was working in only had 2.43.0, and ran it against a handful of conflicts I created on purpose.

The core promise held up. The safety check around it had a gap I didn't expect.

Setting it up

Git 2.56.0 isn't in Ubuntu's repositories yet, so I built it from the kernel.org tarball:

$ ./configure --prefix=$HOME/git-2.56
$ make -j4 NO_GETTEXT=1 NO_TCLTK=1 NO_CURL=1
$ make install NO_GETTEXT=1 NO_TCLTK=1 NO_CURL=1
$ ./git-2.56/bin/git --version
git version 2.56.0

I skipped curl and gettext support because the testing only needed local commands. git add -h confirmed the flag is there:

    --[no-]resolved       add conflict-resolved tracked files

The core promise: it does ignore unrelated files

I built a repo with two branches that both edit file1.txt and file2.txt, merged them to force a conflict, resolved both files properly, and then made an unrelated edit to a third file, file4.txt, that had nothing to do with the merge.

Command file1.txt (resolved) file2.txt (resolved) file4.txt (unrelated edit)
git add . staged staged staged
git add --resolved . staged staged left unstaged

That's the whole pitch, and it's real. After git add --resolved ., git status --short showed:

M  file1.txt
M  file2.txt
 M file4.txt

The leading column is the staged state and the second is the working-tree state. file4.txt has a space in the first column, meaning nothing about it is staged. With plain git add . on the same working tree, all three files come back M in the index column. If you've ever committed a stray console.log or a half-finished change because it happened to be sitting in the tree during a conflict resolution, this removes that failure mode outright.

What it refuses, and what I got wrong on the way

The second claim is that --resolved checks the paths it's about to stage for leftover <<<<<<< markers and aborts if it finds any. My first attempt to test this looked like it had found a bug: I resolved one file, left markers in the other on purpose, ran the command, and got exit code 0 with nothing printed and nothing staged.

That looked like a silent no-op where the documentation promised an error. It wasn't. The problem was my test harness, not the flag. In the run before that one, I had already run git add --resolved . successfully once on that same working tree and then called git reset to put things back for the next scenario. git reset rewrites the index against HEAD, and in doing so it collapses the unmerged (stage 1/2/3) entries into ordinary staged-then-unstaged entries. By the time I reintroduced the markers, git no longer considered those paths unmerged at all, so --resolved had nothing to look at and correctly did nothing. I was testing a file that looked conflicted to a human and wasn't conflicted to git.

Once I rebuilt the conflict from scratch instead of reusing a reset repo, the refusal showed up exactly as documented:

$ git add --resolved .
fatal: the following paths still have conflict markers:
    file2.txt

Exit code 128. And it's atomic: file1.txt was fully and correctly resolved in that same run, but it stayed UU in the index alongside the broken file2.txt. --resolved does not partially stage the paths it's happy with; one bad file blocks the whole invocation. Only after I actually removed the markers from file2.txt did the second run stage both files.

The gap: the check only applies while git calls a file unmerged

The accidental discovery above pointed at something real, so I tested it on purpose. I merged two branches with one conflicting file, left the file with genuine, un-removed <<<<<<< markers, and ran git add --resolved -v . against it while there was no merge in progress and no unmerged entry for that path at all — just an ordinary tracked file with marker text sitting inside it from an earlier git reset.

$ git status --short
 M file1.txt
$ git add --resolved -v .
$ echo exit: $?
exit: 0

No output, even with -v. Nothing staged. The file still contains real <<<<<<< and ======= and >>>>>>> lines, and --resolved walked straight past it, because the only thing it checks is whether the path is in conflict stages in the index right now, not whether the file's content looks like a conflict. The marker scan is a guard on top of "this file is still unmerged," not a general scan for marker text in tracked files. If you've already run any add/reset sequence that clears the unmerged bit — including, ironically, a first successful use of --resolved itself followed by amending something — the safety net is gone and the next --resolved call will happily do nothing, silently, on a file that still has markers in it.

The other gap: it doesn't look inside a file

I then resolved a conflict and, in the same edit, added one extra unrelated line to the same file, to see whether --resolved could tell the two apart:

 line1
 main change
+A change
+UNRELATED DEBUG LINE I FORGOT TO REMOVE

git add --resolved . staged this without complaint. The flag's unit of "unrelated" is the file, not the line. It stops you from staging file4.txt because it's a different path. It will not stop you from staging a debug line you left in the middle of the file you were actually supposed to be fixing.

What it costs

I timed git add --resolved . against plain git add . on a repo with 3,000 genuinely conflicting files, all pre-resolved, five runs each:

Run add --resolved add
1 0.202s 0.196s
2 0.223s 1.404s
3 0.202s 0.230s
4 0.439s 0.168s
5 0.820s 0.175s

The spread swamps the difference. I expected scanning every conflicted file's content for marker strings to show up as a consistent tax on top of ordinary staging, and it didn't: the two distributions overlap, and the single slowest run in the whole table (1.4s) belongs to plain add, not --resolved. On this machine, at this scale, the marker check is not a cost worth worrying about.

Run it yourself 

#!/bin/bash
set -e
GIT=/path/to/git-2.56/bin/git
$GIT init -q -b main repo && cd repo
$GIT config user.email t@t.com && $GIT config user.name T
echo base > a.txt; echo base > b.txt
$GIT add . && $GIT commit -q -m base
$GIT checkout -q -b branchA
echo "A change" >> a.txt; echo "A change" >> b.txt
$GIT commit -q -am branchA
$GIT checkout -q main
echo "main change" >> a.txt; echo "main change" >> b.txt
echo "unrelated edit" >> c.txt
$GIT commit -q -am main
set +e
$GIT merge branchA  # conflicts in a.txt and b.txt
set -e

# resolve a.txt and b.txt by hand:
printf "base\nmain change\nA change\n" > a.txt
printf "base\nmain change\nA change\n" > b.txt

$GIT add --resolved .
$GIT status --short   # c.txt stays unstaged

I ran this exact sequence while writing the post and it produces the table above.

What to do with this

If your merge workflow still ends in git add ., switching to git add --resolved removes a real failure mode: unrelated dirty files no longer ride along into the merge commit, for free, with no measurable cost. Don't treat the marker check as a general-purpose guard against committing broken conflict markers, though. It only fires while git's index still thinks the path is unmerged. If you've run any sequence that clears that state — a reset, an aborted add, a rebase that re-touches the same path — check the file yourself before you commit, because --resolved will not catch it, and it will not tell you it didn't.

articles.title: Rust Doesn't Have a Garbage Collector. It Has Something Stranger.
articles.description: A visual guide to how Rust's compiler proves your memory is safe before your program ever runs. No garbage collector, no manual free(), no runtime cost.
articles.body_html:
Every language you have used solves the same problem: who cleans up the memory?

In C, the answer is you. You call malloc, you call free, and if you forget, your program leaks memory until it crashes. If you free too early, you get a use-after-free bug, the kind of vulnerability that has caused real-world security exploits for three decades.

In Java, Python, and Go, the answer is a garbage collector. A background process scans your heap at runtime, finds objects nobody points to anymore, and reclaims their memory. It works, but it comes at a cost: unpredictable pauses, extra CPU cycles, and a runtime that your compiled binary must carry everywhere.

Rust looked at both approaches and said: neither.

Rust has no garbage collector. It also does not ask you to manually free memory. Instead, the Rust compiler mathematically proves, before your program ever runs, that every piece of memory will be freed at exactly the right moment, exactly once, with zero runtime overhead.

The mechanism behind this is called the ownership system, and it is unlike anything in mainstream programming.

The Three Rules That Replace a Garbage Collector

Rust's entire memory model rests on three rules enforced at compile time:

  1. Every value in Rust has exactly one owner.
  2. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (its memory is freed).
  3. You can temporarily borrow a value, but the compiler tracks every borrow to make sure nothing conflicts.

That sounds simple. Almost suspiciously simple. But these three rules are powerful enough to prevent use-after-free, double-free, dangling pointers, and data races, all without a single byte of runtime overhead.

Let us see exactly how.

Rule 1: One Owner, One Cleanup Responsibility

Consider this Rust code:

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("hello");
    let s2 = s;
    println!("{}", s); // ← This line will NOT compile.
}

If you come from Python or JavaScript, that code looks perfectly fine. You made a string, assigned it to another variable, and tried to print the original. What could go wrong?

In Rust, this fails to compile with the error:

error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s`

Here is what happened. String::from("hello") allocated memory on the heap to store the text. The variable s became the owner of that heap allocation. When you wrote let s2 = s, Rust did not copy the heap data. It moved ownership from s to s2.

After the move, s is no longer valid. The compiler marks it as dead. If you try to use s after the move, the compiler refuses, because allowing that would create two variables pointing at the same heap memory, and when both go out of scope, the runtime would try to free the same block twice.

This is the key insight: Rust does not need a garbage collector because ownership makes the cleanup point deterministic. The compiler knows exactly when each value's owner leaves scope, so it inserts the deallocation call right there, automatically, at compile time.

Rule 2: Borrowing Instead of Sharing

If ownership always moved, Rust would be unusable. Every function call would consume its arguments.

So Rust lets you borrow a value using references:

fn print_length(s: &String) {
    println!("Length: {}", s.len());
}

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("hello");
    print_length(&s);       // Borrow s, don't move it.
    println!("{}", s);       // s is still valid here.
}

The & symbol creates a reference, a temporary, read-only view of the data. The function print_length borrows s but does not own it. When print_length returns, the borrow ends, and s remains valid in main.

But here is where Rust gets strict. The compiler enforces a fundamental aliasing rule:

At any given time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references. Never both.

fn main() {
    let mut s = String::from("hello");

    let r1 = &s;       // Immutable borrow — fine.
    let r2 = &s;       // Another immutable borrow — still fine.
    let r3 = &mut s;   // Mutable borrow — COMPILE ERROR.
}

Why does the compiler care? Because this rule prevents data races at compile time. If two parts of your code could read a value while a third part is modifying it, the program behavior becomes unpredictable. Languages with garbage collectors allow this and rely on the programmer to add locks. Rust makes it structurally impossible.

What the Compiler Actually Builds

Most tutorials stop at the rules. But understanding how the compiler enforces those rules reveals why the system works with zero runtime cost.

When you run cargo build, your Rust source code passes through a pipeline of transformations:

The critical stage is MIR, the Mid-level Intermediate Representation. Before your code reaches MIR, the compiler has already parsed the syntax (AST), desugared complex expressions (HIR), and resolved all types. But ownership and borrowing have not been checked yet.

MIR represents your program as a control-flow graph: a network of basic blocks connected by branches. Each block contains simple, flat statements. No nested expressions, no hidden control flow.

Here is a simplified view of what MIR looks like for a small function:

bb0: {
    _1 = String::from("hello")   // allocate
    _2 = move _1                 // ownership transfers
    drop(_2)                     // compiler inserts cleanup
    return
}

Notice the word move. In MIR, every ownership transfer is explicit. The compiler can now walk this graph and track exactly which variable owns each value at every point in the program.

This is where the borrow checker runs. It performs dataflow analysis on the MIR, tracing every value's lifetime, every borrow's span, and every move. If the analysis finds a conflict, it rejects the program with a compile error.

If no conflicts exist, the compiler knows something powerful: every value will be freed exactly once, at a known location, and no reference will ever outlive its data.

The safety proof is complete. Everything after this point is pure optimization.

The "Zero-Cost" Part: What Reaches the CPU

After the borrow checker approves your code, the MIR is translated into LLVM IR and handed to the LLVM optimization engine, the same backend used by Clang for C and C++.

By this point, the ownership rules have already been enforced. LLVM does not know or care about Rust's borrow checker. It sees ordinary code with explicit allocation and deallocation points, and it optimizes the result like any other systems language.

Consider this function:

fn sum_lengths(a: &str, b: &str) -> usize {
    a.len() + b.len()
}

No heap allocation. No reference counting. No garbage collector scan. The compiler verifies the borrows at compile time, and the generated machine code is a plain addition of two integers. The abstraction evaporated completely.

This is what Rust means by "zero-cost abstractions": the safety checks happen during compilation and leave no trace in the final binary. Your program runs as fast as an equivalent C program, but the compiler has already proven it cannot corrupt memory.

Lifetimes: The Compiler's Invisible Bookkeeping

Sometimes the borrow checker needs help figuring out how long a reference should live. That is where lifetime annotations appear:

fn longer<'a>(s1: &'a str, s2: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if s1.len() > s2.len() { s1 } else { s2 }
}

The 'a annotation does not change your program's behavior. It is a hint to the borrow checker: "the returned reference lives at least as long as both input references."

This lets the compiler verify, at compile time, that the caller does not use the returned reference after either s1 or s2 has been freed. If it cannot prove safety, it refuses to compile.

Lifetime annotations are not runtime markers. They are erased during compilation, just like the ownership checks. They exist only to help the compiler complete its proof.

Most of the time, you never write them. Rust has lifetime elision rules that infer the common patterns automatically. You only need explicit annotations when the compiler genuinely cannot determine the relationships on its own.

When Ownership Is Not Enough

Rust's ownership system covers the vast majority of programs, but it has limits. Some data structures, like graphs or doubly-linked lists, require multiple owners by design. The compiler's single-owner rule would make them impossible to express.

For these cases, Rust provides opt-in runtime mechanisms:

  • Rc<T> (Reference Counting): Tracks the number of owners at runtime. When the count reaches zero, the value is dropped. Single-threaded only.
  • Arc<T> (Atomic Reference Counting): Like Rc, but safe to share across threads using atomic operations.
  • RefCell<T>: Moves borrow checking from compile time to runtime. Panics if you violate the aliasing rules.

These types carry a small runtime cost, which is why they are explicit and opt-in. Rust does not hide the cost. You choose exactly where to pay it, and the compiler enforces everything else for free.

Why This Matters Beyond Rust

The ownership model is not just a language feature. It represents a fundamentally different answer to a problem every programmer faces.

C and C++ gave the programmer full control and full responsibility. Entire classes of security vulnerabilities, buffer overflows, use-after-free, dangling pointers, exist because humans make mistakes with manual memory management. Microsoft estimated that roughly 70% of their security vulnerabilities were caused by memory safety issues.

Garbage-collected languages solved safety by adding a runtime process. That works, but it introduces latency spikes, higher memory usage, and a floor on performance that no amount of tuning can fully remove.

Rust found a third path: prove safety at compile time and generate code with no overhead. The tradeoff is compilation time and a steeper learning curve. The borrow checker requires you to think about data ownership explicitly, something that most languages let you ignore.

But once you internalize the model, the compiler stops being an obstacle and starts acting as a collaborator that catches entire categories of bugs before your code ever executes.

If you have tried Rust and hit a wall with the borrow checker, try looking at it from the compiler's perspective. It is not being difficult. It is building a mathematical proof that your program cannot corrupt memory, and it is asking you for enough information to finish that proof. Once you see the errors through that lens, they start making sense.

What was the first Rust compiler error that genuinely surprised you? And if you have not tried Rust yet, what is the one thing that still feels intimidating about it?

References:

  • The Rust Programming Language, Chapter 4: Understanding Ownership (Official Rust Book)
  • Rust Compiler Development Guide: MIR
  • Rust Compiler Development Guide: The Borrow Checker
  • Microsoft Security Response Center: Memory Safety (70% of CVEs are memory safety issues)

articles.title: C# Without a Project File: File-Based Apps in .NET 11 (a 5-Minute Refresh)
articles.description: Since .NET 10 you can run a C# file without a project: dotnet run app.cs. No .sln, no .csproj. But it...
articles.body_html:
Since .NET 10 you can run a C# file without a project: dotnet run app.cs. No .sln, no .csproj. But it was one file only. In .NET 11 a file-based app can have many files, and that makes it useful for real small tools.

I tried it on the classic Mars Rover kata. A rover starts at 0 0 N. L and R turn 90°, M moves one cell forward. The program prints the final position.


The real Mars rover: Perseverance, with the Ingenuity helicopter behind it. Ours only knows L, R and M. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS

Here is what we'll go through:

  1. One file: run C# without a project
  2. #:include: split the app into files
  3. Nested includes: a file that includes other files
  4. Settings: read a JSON file, and watch it crash
  5. Native AOT: turn it off, or use the JSON source generator

1. One file: run C# without a project 

// app.cs
Console.WriteLine("Rover is ready");

dotnet run app.cs

That's all. The SDK creates a hidden project for you.

2. #:include: split the app into files

Move the rover logic to its own file, and include it from app.cs:

mars-rover/
├── app.cs
├── settings.json
├── rover/rover.cs
└── helpers/directions.cs

// app.cs
#:include rover/rover.cs

var rover = new Rover(0, 0, "N");
rover.Execute("LMLMLMLMM");
Console.WriteLine(rover);   // 0 1 N

One rule: only the entry file (app.cs) can have top-level statements. Included files only add types.

3. Nested includes: a file that includes other files

The rover includes the directions helper itself, so app.cs doesn't need to know about it:

// rover/rover.cs
#:include ../helpers/directions.cs

class Rover(int x, int y, string facing)
{
    int _x = x, _y = y;
    int _dir = Directions.IndexOf(facing);

    public void Execute(string commands)
    {
        foreach (var c in commands)
        {
            switch (c)
            {
                case 'L': _dir = Directions.Left(_dir); break;
                case 'R': _dir = Directions.Right(_dir); break;
                case 'M':
                    var (dx, dy) = Directions.Delta(_dir);
                    _x += dx; _y += dy;
                    break;
                default: throw new ArgumentException($"Unknown command: {c}");
            }
        }
    }

    public override string ToString() => $"{_x} {_y} {Directions.Name(_dir)}";
}

// helpers/directions.cs
static class Directions
{
    const string Ring = "NESW";   // clockwise
    static readonly (int, int)[] Deltas = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)];

    public static int IndexOf(string f) =>
        Ring.IndexOf(f) is var i and >= 0 && f.Length == 1 ? i : throw new ArgumentException($"Unknown direction: {f}");

    public static int Left(int d) => (d + 3) % 4;
    public static int Right(int d) => (d + 1) % 4;
    public static (int, int) Delta(int d) => Deltas[d];
    public static char Name(int d) => Ring[d];
}

Each file says what it needs, like a using, but for files.

4. Settings: read a JSON file, and watch it crash

Put the start position in settings.json:

{ "X": 0, "Y": 0, "Facing": "N" }

Read it from the folder of app.cs, so it works wherever you run the app from:

var dir = AppContext.GetData("EntryPointFileDirectoryPath") as string ?? ".";
var json = File.ReadAllText(Path.Combine(dir, "settings.json"));
var start = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Start>(json)!;

record Start(int X, int Y, string Facing);

Run it, and it crashes:

System.InvalidOperationException:
Reflection-based serialization has been disabled for this application.

5. Native AOT: turn it off, or use the JSON source generator

File-based apps have Native AOT on by default, and AOT turns off reflection-based JSON. You have two options.

Option A: turn AOT off. Add one line at the top, and the code from step 4 works as is:

#:property PublishAot=false

Option B: keep AOT, use the JSON source generator. A few more lines, but you keep the fast startup and the native binary:

#!/usr/bin/env dotnet
#:include rover/rover.cs

using System.Text.Json;
using System.Text.Json.Serialization;

var dir = AppContext.GetData("EntryPointFileDirectoryPath") as string ?? ".";
var json = File.ReadAllText(Path.Combine(dir, "settings.json"));
var start = JsonSerializer.Deserialize(json, AppJson.Default.Start)!;

var rover = new Rover(start.X, start.Y, start.Facing);
rover.Execute(args.Length > 0 ? args[0] : "LMLMLMLMM");
Console.WriteLine(rover);

record Start(int X, int Y, string Facing);

[JsonSerializable(typeof(Start))]
partial class AppJson : JsonSerializerContext;

$ dotnet run app.cs
0 1 N
$ dotnet run app.cs -- RRMMLM
1 -2 E

For a quick tool, A is fine. If startup time matters, choose B. The #! line on top removes analyzer warning CA2266, and on macOS/Linux it lets you run chmod +x app.cs && ./app.cs.

Notes for later

  1. dotnet run app.cs runs a C# file without a project.
  2. #:include path.cs adds another file (.NET 11).
  3. Included files can include other files. Only the entry file has top-level code.
  4. EntryPointFileDirectoryPath gives you the folder of your app file.
  5. AOT is on by default: use #:property PublishAot=false or the JSON source generator.

Would you use this for small tools, or stay with projects? Tell me in comments. 🙂

articles.title: Is Coding with AI Actually Faster and Cheaper?
articles.description: How has AI actually changed the way we work? Are coding agents really making us remarkably faster?...
articles.body_html:
How has AI actually changed the way we work? Are coding agents really making us remarkably faster? And what if, instead of answering with “well, that's what I think,” we tried looking at some actual scientific research?

This is another article inspired by the upcoming AI Coding Summit in Berlin (and yes, I'll leave a link to my speaker badge at the end again, which I think might come with some discounts). I promised myself I wouldn't do this again, but, as usual, I've also signed up for three panel discussions. 😅 One of them has a title very similar to this article.

I wanted some hard data for that discussion, so I dug into the research. You'll find links to all the studies at the end.

And since today hasn't exactly been a great day for me, and I'd much rather be somewhere else, I figured I'd cheer myself up the usual way. By writing something for you!

Are we actually coding faster?

Let's start with the first question. Has AI really made us faster? If someone suddenly stopped me in the street and demanded an answer, I'd probably say yes. In my experience, we write code much faster now.

But that improvement doesn't seem to translate into an equally dramatic increase in how much software we actually deliver. After all, there's code review, analysis, discussions, and so on and so on. Sure, things are a bit faster. Maybe a little less stressful, too. But I wouldn't say the entire development process has suddenly become much quicker.

Then again, maybe it's just me? Maybe the rest of the world is already shipping features at the speed of light?

Well, apparently not.

A study by economists from MIT and Wharton, revised in September 2026, suggests that my intuition might not be entirely wrong. The researchers analyzed data from more than 500,000 GitHub developers and estimated the following cumulative changes associated with autonomous coding agents:

Metric Estimated change
Coding activity (commits) +240%
Software releases +30%
Total app usage across the marketplaces studied No overall increase

These are observational estimates. Still, the gap between the jump in commits and the increase in releases is pretty striking.

Okay, so we're committing a lot more and shipping somewhat more often. In my own work, it sometimes just feels a little less stressful. But it's hardly the revolution some people make it out to be. Maybe things look different in brand-new projects. In large, established systems like the ones I work on, I haven't seen anything close to a tenfold improvement.

Maybe that'll change when someone invents those super-self-healing-autonomous agents. For now, I sometimes feel like things are getting more complicated. With everything that's been happening around AI security lately, everyone seems to be getting a little obsessed with it. Myself very much included. 😅

But are individual developers actually faster?

Okay, we have more commits. But are we actually coding faster? Again, if I had to guess, I'd say yes, but not that much faster.

The data is mixed.

Study Result What was measured
Cui et al., Management Science, 2026 +26.08% Number of completed tasks
METR, July 2025 19% slower Time to complete tasks
Science, January 2026 +3.6% Estimated increase in quarterly coding activity on GitHub
Borg et al., June 2026 30.7% less time Median reduction in implementation time in the observational phase

Once again, the results are reasonably close to what I expected. I'm not going to spend the next ten paragraphs going over the methodology. If you're curious, the original studies are linked below. They looked at different developers, tools, and tasks, and each percentage measures something different.

Several of these studies do point to gains, though. We're not all suddenly 10x developers. xD But there are real improvements.

METR is the odd one out here. It's from 2025, which, in the current AI world, practically makes it ancient history. But I love one detail about it.

Before the experiment, developers expected AI to make them about 24% faster. The actual result? They were 19% slower! And even after the experiment, they still thought AI had made them faster.

It shows how much we can fool ourselves until we actually measure things. I swear, this applies to practically every area of life. For example, I used to think I barely ate anything. 😂

To be fair, METR published an update in February 2026. The researchers think newer tools are likely to be more helpful, but their follow-up couldn't reliably estimate the speedup because of who was willing to participate.

Okay, but is software development actually cheaper?

If someone woke me up at midnight and asked whether AI had made software development cheaper, I'd probably say no. At least not yet.

The 2025 DORA research and a follow-up published in March 2026 point to something many of us have written about. Some of the time we save writing code goes straight into auditing and verifying it. So the savings on implementation can shrink by the time the change gets to production. DORA describes where that work can shift, leaving the overall cost question open.

Yes, yes, I've heard about multi-agent teams where one agent writes the code, another reviews it, another tests it, and then it all goes into production. I'm sure that can work in some situations. I'd be very cautious about trying that trick in a mission-critical system. Financial software, for example. Good luck with that strategy 😂🤞

What about the cost of tokens?

One last question. Are we spending all the money we save by writing code faster on tokens?

I have to admit, the answer surprised me! If I had to guess, I'd have said yes, especially if you blindly use the most expensive models for absolutely everything.

But the findings are more interesting than that! Two recent studies looked at the economics of AI-assisted software development. One was published in September 2026 by Potluri and colleagues, and the other in October 2026 by Steffen Herbold.

Both suggest that the effectiveness of an AI agent can matter more than the price of the tokens it consumes. In Potluri's analysis, models that solved more tasks produced substantial estimated savings, while less effective models ended up costing more in many task categories. A cheap model can get expensive pretty quickly if it keeps failing and you have to pay for another try.

Herbold simulated 432 scenarios for teams using a mix of developers and AI agents. He included salaries, token costs, supervision, bugs, and technical debt. Teams with highly capable agents were usually cheaper than teams of developers working without AI. The results for less capable agents were mixed. In the simulation, agent capability mattered more than token price because better results cut the cost of checking and fixing the work.

Herbold's results come from simulations, and Potluri's estimates come from benchmarks and economic modeling. So we have two ways of estimating when the savings might outweigh the token bill. The actual cost of building and maintaining commercial software is a much bigger question.

So, what's the verdict?

It looks like AI really can make coding faster and cheaper. Several studies show gains on specific tasks, and the economic models suggest that capable agents can save money even after you pay for the tokens.

We still have less evidence about whether the total cost of building, delivering, securing, and maintaining software has fallen across the industry.

So far, the research mostly lines up with what a lot of us seem to feel. Skynet may already be sharpening its weapons, but it hasn't conquered the world just yet. 😅

And what about you? Do these findings reflect your experience? Has AI genuinely made your team faster and cheaper, or does it look completely different where you work?

I'd love to hear your thoughts!

If you enjoyed this article, you can also follow me on LinkedIn.

And if you'd like access to free materials from AI Coding Summit, you can register using my speaker badge.

articles.title: Twelve Files for Twenty Lines: When Clean Code Becomes the Problem
articles.description: I've seen perfectly clean code that nobody could change. Over-engineering dresses up as good practice. Here's how I tell the difference, what it costs in cognitive load, and the ugly function I now defend in review.
articles.body_html:
I've seen code that ticked every box. Small functions. One responsibility per class. Interfaces everywhere. Not a single line you could call ugly.

And nobody could change it.

I remember one ticket: add an optional phone number to a form. We estimated half a day. It took three, and twelve files. Most of that time didn't go into changing the code. It went into finding where things happened.

To understand what happened when a user clicked "Save", you had to follow six jumps: a handler that called a service that called a factory that built a strategy that delegated to a mapper that finally touched the data. Twenty lines of real logic, spread thin over an architecture built for a future that never came.

Everyone who had written it was proud of it. Everyone who had to maintain it was afraid of it. Not because any piece was hard. Because you had to hold all of them in your head at once.

We don't talk about this enough. We have a hundred articles on how to clean up messy code. We have very few on the opposite failure, because the opposite failure looks like virtue.

What it looks like

Here's an illustration. Not real code from a real project, but if you've been around, you've met its cousins.

The task: apply a discount to an order if the customer is a member.

// DiscountStrategy.ts
export interface DiscountStrategy {
  apply(amount: number): number
}

// MemberDiscountStrategy.ts
export class MemberDiscountStrategy implements DiscountStrategy {
  apply(amount: number) { return amount * 0.9 }
}

// NoDiscountStrategy.ts
export class NoDiscountStrategy implements DiscountStrategy {
  apply(amount: number) { return amount }
}

// DiscountStrategyFactory.ts
export class DiscountStrategyFactory {
  create(customer: Customer): DiscountStrategy {
    return customer.isMember
      ? new MemberDiscountStrategy()
      : new NoDiscountStrategy()
  }
}

// OrderPricingService.ts
export class OrderPricingService {
  constructor(private factory: DiscountStrategyFactory) {}
  price(order: Order) {
    return this.factory.create(order.customer).apply(order.amount)
  }
}

Five files. Every one of them is "clean". Each class has one job, each name is honest, each piece is testable alone.

And here's the same thing:

function priceOf(order: Order) {
  const discount = order.customer.isMember ? 0.9 : 1
  return order.amount * discount
}

Three lines. You read it once and you know everything.

"But what if we add more discount types?" Then you'll change it, on the day you add them, knowing what they actually look like. Which is almost never what you imagined a year before.

The cost nobody measures

Count the files and you still miss the real price. The real price is paid in your head.

To read the three-line version, you hold one thing in mind. To read the five-file version, you hold five: the interface, the two strategies, the factory, the service, and how they connect. None of them is hard. But you have to keep all of them loaded at once to answer one question: what does a member pay?

That's cognitive load, and to me it's the main problem with this kind of code. Working memory is small. Every jump spends some of it on the structure instead of on the problem. By the sixth jump, you've forgotten why you opened the first file.

No linter reports it. No coverage tool measures it. It shows up elsewhere: in onboarding that takes months, in estimates that double, in the bug nobody wants to pick up.

"AI will handle it"

I hear this more and more. The model writes the twelve files in seconds, and it can walk you through them too. So who cares about the indirection?

I do. Typing was never the bottleneck. Understanding is. AI makes structure cheap to produce, which makes it cheap to produce more structure than anyone can hold in their head.

This part is personal opinion: the day you lose your grip on your own code, you lose the core of the job. My test is simple. When someone tells me "it's broken here", I want to know right away which file to open, where to put the breakpoint, what to test. If I need a tool to explain my own codebase before I can start debugging, it isn't really my code anymore.

Why we do it

I've been that developer. I think most of us have, right after we discovered design patterns.

The first reason is that rules are easier than judgment. "Functions should be short" can be checked by a linter. "This code should be easy to change" can't. So we optimize what we can measure, and a codebase can score perfectly on every rule and still be miserable to work in.

The second is fear. An abstraction "just in case" feels like insurance. It isn't. Insurance pays when the accident happens. A speculative abstraction costs you every day, and when the real requirement arrives, it's usually the wrong shape, and now you have to undo it first.

The third is harder to admit. Elegant code is satisfying to write. That's not a crime. But the reader doesn't get the pleasure. They only get the indirection.

How I tell the difference now

Clean code isn't the code that ticks the most rules. It's the code the next developer understands quickly and changes without fear.

So I've replaced the rules with four questions:

  1. How many files do I open to change one behavior? If the answer is more than two or three for a small change, the structure is working against me.
  2. Can I point to the second use? An interface with one implementation is a question, not an answer. I want to see the second caller before I build for it.
  3. Could a newcomer follow it in one sitting? If understanding a click takes six jumps, the code isn't clean. It's hidden.
  4. When it breaks, do I know which file to open? If a bug report doesn't point me somewhere within seconds, I've lost the map of my own code.

And a habit that follows from them: sometimes I defend the ugly function. Thirty lines, top to bottom, a few ifs, readable at a glance. In review, someone suggests splitting it into five. I ask what we gain, and who it's for.

Sometimes the answer is good, and we split it. Often there isn't one.

What finally got that codebase simplified wasn't a refactoring plan. A new developer joined, spent two weeks on a one-line fix, and asked in a retro why saving a form needed six classes. Nobody in the room had a good answer. So we started inlining, one flow at a time, each time we had to touch one.

What I'm not saying

I'm not saying patterns are bad, or that a 400-line function is fine. I wrote a whole article about the principles I code by, and I stand by them. KISS and YAGNI are on that list for a reason: they're the two principles that protect you from the others.

The goal was never beauty. It's maintainability. Most of the time they agree. When they don't, I know which one I'm paid for.

Have you ever worked in code that was too clean to maintain? What did it look like, and what finally got it simplified? And does AI change the answer for you?

I write about front-end architecture and modernizing legacy code. More on my site. Let's talk on LinkedIn.
