If you've been scrolling through X or GitHub lately, you've probably seen msitarzewski/agency-agents pop up in your feed. Whenever a repo starts trending like this, people usually hype it up like it's some brand new AI breakthrough, so to be clear upfront: it's not a new model, a runtime framework, or a standalone coding tool. It's literally just a public repository full of markdown files containing detailed system prompts.

That said, once you look past the hype, it's actually pretty useful—especially if you're tired of writing your own custom instructions from scratch or if your coding assistant keeps agreeing with every bad architectural idea you throw at it.

What's actually in the repo

Most prompt repositories on GitHub are filled with generic one-liners like "act as a senior engineer and write clean code." Those rarely change how an LLM behaves once you get past the first two messages.

agency-agents takes a different approach by organizing over a hundred multi-page markdown files into clear categories (engineering, testing, design, product, etc.). Instead of vague encouragement, each file outlines specific rules, edge cases to watch out for, formatting expectations, and explicit instructions on when the model should push back.

For example, if you're refactoring a messy script or designing a new data pipeline, you can load up the reality-checker.md or software-architect.md file. Instead of blindly generating boilerplate and telling you every idea is great, the model actually critiques your structure, points out potential bottlenecks, and forces you to simplify things before writing code.

How to set it up locally

Since everything in the repo is just plain text, there are no dependencies to install, no Docker containers to spin up, and no background daemons eating RAM. You just clone the repository somewhere permanent on your machine and point whatever tool you already use to the specific file you need.

1. Clone the repo locally 

git clone https://github.com/msitarzewski/agency-agents.git ~/.local/share/agency-agents

2. Pick a file and wire it into your tool

Depending on your workflow, you just symlink or copy the markdown file into your project directory:

  • Claude Code / CLI workflows: Symlink the file to CLAUDE.md in your project root so it loads automatically when you start a session (just make sure to add CLAUDE.md to your .gitignore if you're working on a shared repo): 
  ln -s ~/.local/share/agency-agents/engineering/software-architect.md ./CLAUDE.md
  • Cursor / Windsurf: Copy or symlink the .md file straight into your project's .cursor/rules/ directory.
  • Local models (Ollama / llama.cpp): If you run models locally in the terminal, you can pass the file contents directly into your system prompt flag: 
  llama-cli -m your-model.gguf --system-prompt "$(cat ~/.local/share/agency-agents/testing/reality-checker.md)" -p "Review this code"
  • Neovim / Editor plugins: If you use local AI plugins like Avante, CodeCompanion, or similar setups, you can simply point your custom system prompt path to whichever .md file fits the task you're working on.

(There's also a small Tauri app called agency-agents-app linked in the repo if you prefer clicking through a GUI to copy them into your editor configs, though symlinking in the terminal takes two seconds).

A practical way to use it without clutter

The easiest mistake to make with a repo this big is trying to combine multiple personas at once or keeping a heavy system prompt active all the time.

A better workflow is swapping them out depending on what phase of a project you're in. Use a planning or architecture persona when you're mapping out how components talk to each other, switch to a standard implementation prompt while writing the actual functions, and then swap in a testing or reality-checker file right before you commit to catch edge cases you missed. Because they're just symlinks, switching roles takes a single terminal command.

Worth keeping in mind

At the end of the day, it's still just prompt engineering. If you're running a smaller local model with a tight context window, loading a 2,000-word markdown file will eat up a noticeable chunk of your token budget before you even paste your code. It works best when you pick one focused role for the exact problem in front of you, or trim down the markdown files to keep only the rules relevant to your stack.

Curious if anyone else here keeps a local folder of system prompts like this, or if you've found better repos worth cloning.

About the Author

I write about artificial intelligence, software engineering, emerging developer tools, and the technologies shaping how modern products are built.

Interested in collaborating?

If you're a company or team working in AI or developer technology, I'd love to hear about what you're building. I'm always interested in discovering new projects and sharing technologies that I genuinely find useful with my readers.

You can reach me at maamrihayder@gmail.com.

articles.title: Coding Agents Keep Installing the Old Version of Your Library
articles.description: I work on helping coding agents write better code, and one question keeps coming back. Libraries...
articles.body_html:
I work on helping coding agents write better code, and one question keeps coming back. Libraries change fast: a new major, a renamed package, an API that is gone. Do agents move to the new version as willingly as a developer who reads the release notes, and do they use it as well? If you maintain a library that changed this year, the answer decides what code your users get when they ask an agent for it.

To find out, I took 20 libraries that changed in 2026, most with a new major, a rename or a removed API, and for two weeks gave Claude Code, Codex and Gemini the jobs their users would give them: add "the current" SDK to a small project, upgrade an app to the new major, write code against an API that changed. Each agent did every task several times. A hidden grader checked the code, and a log recorded everything the agent opened.

That came to 34 checks and 433 graded runs. Often the agents did not move. In 31 of the 34 checks they got something wrong in a way the library could fix. Usually the code ran fine on the old version, and the agent told the user it was current.

Asked for "the current version", agents ended on it in 32 of 66 runs

These are the 11 libraries where an agent could install the wrong version: the old package was still latest, the user used the old name, or the old API was still in the package. For the other 9, the new version was what npm or PyPI installed anyway, so the test was the code written against it. Runs on the current version, out of 6 per library: Claude Code, Codex and Gemini, 2 runs each, nothing pointing to the docs.

Below is what happened, in the order an agent meets your library: npm first, then the files on disk, then the docs. The changes that moved the numbers are collected in a checklist at the end.

The test

Each check is one task, worded the way a user would ask, with nothing in the prompt that points to the docs. The task never names the version: "the current version from npm", "upgrade to the current Video.js". Each agent gets a fresh project, web access, full shell and 25 minutes. A script grades the result: which package and version ended up in the code, whether it builds and works against a real or fake server, and whether the agent told the user what it did. A second pass reads the log for what the agent opened: npm, the README, type files, docs pages, llms.txt, skills, MCP tools.

Most checks ran each task twice on each of the three agents, 6 runs per check. Where I tested a fix, I reran the same task with one change switched on: a deprecation through a local registry that behaves like npm, a patched README, a few lines in AGENTS.md. Three experiments compare docs channels with 45 runs each. Small samples like these show big effects only; I say so where it matters.

Where agents decide

Before any docs, an agent asked for "the current version" goes to the package registry. It runs npm view or just npm install, and it sees latest, the README and a deprecation notice if there is one. Most of the wrong choices were made right there, in the first minute.

After that it reads what is on disk: type definitions, the README and docs inside node_modules, error messages from the compiler, the CLI or your server. The docs site comes last, and many runs never got there. llms.txt was opened in 0 of 59 runs where nothing pointed to it.

1. Make latest mean the latest

Prisma 8's CLI was already latest on npm as a release candidate, but @prisma/client@latest still pointed to 7.10.1. Three of six runs chose Prisma 7 on purpose: they saw the CLI and the client on different majors and applied an old, correct rule that the two must match. Only 2 of 6 ended on Prisma 8.

OpenCode's v2 server came with a new SDK, but the old @opencode-ai/sdk was still latest on npm. Three of six runs started on the old one, and its calls to the v2 server got back an HTML page with status 200 instead of an error.

The counterexample is Effect. Its v4 went out under the same name with latest pointing at it, so an agent that installed the obvious package got the new version and the docs that ship with it.

When the new major is the one you want people on, move latest to it. If a companion package can't move yet, say so in its README's first line.

2. Deprecate the old package, then ship one last release that says where to go

Hedera moved its JavaScript SDK to @hiero-ledger/sdk, but the old @hashgraph/sdk was still latest, not deprecated, and its README didn't mention the move (issue). All 6 runs built a correct signed transfer on the old package. None opened the agent skill Hedera had published for exactly this.

I simulated the fix with a local registry that serves the old package as deprecated, exactly as npm would. The same task went from 0 of 6 to 3 of 6 on the new package. The logs show why only half switched. npm view old-pkg prints DEPRECATED at the top, and the runs that used it switched. npm view old-pkg version prints only the number, and npm install prints the warning after the choice is made. One run cut the warning off with | tail -5.

Moss had the same shape after renaming its scope: 3 of 6 on the new @moss-js/moss. A simulated npm deprecate brought it to 4 of 6. Deprecation plus one last release of the old package, whose README opens with "moved, same API, install @moss-js/moss", brought it to 6 of 6. That fix takes about ten minutes. If you want to know whether your own package has this problem, there's a 2-minute read-only check your agent can run.

npm deprecate the old package with the new name in the message, then publish a final patch release of it whose README's first line says where it moved.

3. After a rename, agents use the name the user typed

When the user says the old name, agents follow the user. Context.dev used to be Brand.dev. With "Brand.dev" in the prompt, 4 of 6 runs installed the frozen brand.dev package. With "Context.dev", 6 of 6 used the new SDK.

LadybugDB is the maintained fork of Kùzu, which was archived. Asked to use Kùzu, 6 of 6 runs stayed on the archived kuzu package. A fix in LadybugDB's agent skill got 5 of 6 runs to tell the user Kùzu is archived, though 5 of 6 still installed it. LadybugDB merged that change.

The libraries that kept their name had it easier. Video.js 10 ships as new @videojs/* packages, but the old video.js package now contains a redirect that tells you where the player went. All 6 runs asking for "Video.js, current version" ended on v10 (results).

Keep the package name if you can. If you can't, make the old name lead to the new one everywhere a user's word can land: the old package, its README, your skill, your docs search.

4. Put deprecations where the agent reads them

A deprecation that lives only in JSDoc or on the website doesn't reach the agent that's writing code. Rivet 3.0 deprecated c.state in favor of a new API: 3 of 6 runs used c.state, and none told the user. CopilotKit's v1 API is deprecated in favor of v2: both Gemini runs used v1. Charm's Bubble Tea and Lip Gloss moved to v2 under a new module path: both Gemini runs used v1 and called it current.

Mark renamed and removed APIs @deprecated in the type files with the replacement's name. Keep removed names as stubs for a release so the compiler error points to the right thing, and log a warning at run time that names the replacement.

5. Make error messages name the fix

Kestra 2.0 removed ForEach (now Loop) and the json() function (now fromJson()), and an open issue asks for better errors for exactly these. Over 15 runs with no help, 6 wrote one of them. Each got an error that didn't name the replacement: Invalid type: io.kestra.plugin.core.flow.ForEach, or Function or Macro [json] does not exist. They found the answer by listing the server's plugins, and one run spent 25 minutes, part of it unzipping the server's jar. Claude and Gemini never opened Kestra's 2.0 docs at all, so for them the error message was the only 2.0 documentation they saw.

Mem0's upgrade from 1.x to 2.x removed graph memory from the open-source package. None of four runs told the user that it moved to Mem0's platform, and one Codex run wrote its own Neo4j layer to replace it.

Treat errors for removed things as docs. "ForEach was removed in 2.0, use io.kestra.plugin.core.flow.Loop" costs one line and reaches every agent that hits it.

6. Make the documented path work with nobody at the keyboard

Agents run your commands in a terminal nobody watches. Crash Override's CLI wanted an interactive terminal to produce a report (issue), so 6 of 6 runs had to write their own config file to get one. One Prisma run started init without --yes and waited on a prompt until time ran out.

Docs examples get copied word for word. E2B's docs showed install_cmd and run_cmd for a custom MCP server in a sandbox; all 4 runs that got that far wrote them, and the gateway ignores both. CrewAI's docs offer a prompt to paste into your agent for setup: step 6 failed in 6 of 6 runs (issue).

The default settings shaped results too. Asked to start Arize Phoenix 21 in Docker and send it traces, 6 of 6 runs turned authentication off to get it working, and none used an API key.

Show non-interactive flags in every command, make the CLI work without a terminal, run your docs examples in CI, and make the secure path the one that works on the first try.

7. Ship the docs inside the package

What's in node_modules always matches the installed version and is on disk when the agent hits an error. Video.js ships its full docs in @videojs/html, and the runs read them. Effect ships an AGENTS.md and runnable examples in its package, and every run read them or the source.

Put an upgrade note and the main guides in the tarball, with predictable names (UPGRADE.md, docs/, AGENTS.md).

8. Ten lines beat a docs MCP

Three libraries asked, in public, whether they should build a docs MCP or ship a skill. I ran the same task on each with one channel switched on at a time: nothing, a line pointing to the vendor's llms.txt, the vendor's skill, a docs MCP, and 5 to 13 lines from the vendor's own migration guide in the project's AGENTS.md. That's 9 runs per channel on each library, 135 in all.

The short brief was the only channel with a significant effect, and it was never worse than nothing:

  • Camunda 8.10, picking the current Node client: 4 of 9 with nothing, 9 of 9 with the brief (p = 0.03, results).
  • Video.js 10, upgrading a v8 app: everyone got there, but the brief cut tokens and tool calls by about a third (p ≤ 0.001).
  • Kestra 2.0: no channel made a significant difference. With the brief, the llms.txt pointer or the skill, all 9 first attempts used 2.0 constructs; with nothing or the docs MCP, 7 of 9 did.

The others had specific limits. The docs MCP was called in only 16 of 27 runs, and Codex didn't call it in any of its 9: it had the tools listed and searched the web instead. Kestra's hosted MCP also advertises a login that Codex can't complete, so Codex hides its tools (how to check your own MCP server). Skills were read in 27 of 27 runs and gained nothing measurable; on Kestra the skill was the slowest channel. The llms.txt pointer was followed in 23 of 27 runs and helped exactly as much as the page it led to.

AGENTS.md lives in the user's project, so you can't add lines to it yourself. There are two ways to get them there: your CLI can write those lines during setup (@videojs/cli agents init and Camunda's c8ctl setup already write agent files), or your README can offer the block to copy.

Write the 5 to 15 lines an agent needs for your current version first: the package to install, what was removed, the new names. Ship them in the package and in your CLI's setup. Build an MCP after that, and check that each agent actually calls it.

When none of this applies: the models already know your version

If the models already know your new version, the traps above mostly don't fire. Expo's removed module was still latest and undeprecated, the same trap as Hedera, yet 12 of 12 runs used the replacement: it shipped in 2025, and the models had learned it. Ask the models with tools turned off:

claude -p "From memory, no tools: do you know <package> version <N>? Install command and a 10-line example, or say UNKNOWN." --tools ""

If they answer UNKNOWN, your users' agents will decide from npm, from your errors and from what's on disk, and the sections above are the order to fix them in.

Check your library before the next release

Each line is one change from the sections above, in the order an agent meets your library. The first two are npm commands and take minutes.

  1. Point latest at the version you want people on.
  2. Deprecate a renamed package, and ship one last release whose README says where it moved.
  3. Make the old name lead to the new one everywhere a user might type it.
  4. Mark removed APIs @deprecated in the type files, with the replacement's name.
  5. Name the replacement in the error a removed thing throws.
  6. Make every documented command work with nobody at the keyboard.
  7. Ship an upgrade note and your guides inside the package.
  8. Write 5 to 15 lines for AGENTS.md before you build a docs MCP.

You don't have to go through this list by hand. Two ways to have it checked for your own package:

  • Run the 2-minute npm check. It's read-only, and your agent can do it for you.
  • Ask for a check of your next release. You name the task your users give their agents; I run it on Claude Code, Codex and Gemini and send you what each one did.

Limits

Two or three runs per agent per check: these are examples and big effects, not rates. One task per check, in my wording, on my machine. The fixes for Hedera and Moss are simulations through a local registry; the npm website still showed the old state, though no run opened it. Agents and models change every few weeks, so a check is a snapshot with a date.

The data

Every check here has its prompt, the per-run results, a short step-by-step view of what each agent did and the full logs. Each company has them in a private workspace on Ready for Agents, where they can also connect their own agent to read the results and ask the next question.

articles.title: Longer Timeouts Won't Fix Your Webhook Duplicates. Claiming the Work Once Will
articles.description: The receiver was not down. That is the part I keep coming back to. It was answering every single...
articles.body_html:
The receiver was not down. That is the part I keep coming back to. It was answering every single delivery, taking its time about it, two and a half seconds from first byte to done. My sweeper checked once a second for an acknowledgement, heard nothing after one second, and decided the delivery must be lost. It was not lost. It was still being written down at the other end. By the time the first acknowledgement arrived, the same order had already gone out three times.

That was this morning, on my own machine, with one delivery key and a receiver I had deliberately slowed down. krusenas raised this in the comments on "My Cron Job Fired 50 Times While the Receiver Was Down. 10 Webhooks Vanished." He wanted the slow case, not the dead one. What happens when the receiver is up, healthy, and simply a second too slow for the thing watching it? A dead receiver fails loudly. A slow one looks exactly like a dead one for two and a half seconds, and a sweeper that resends on silence will happily manufacture duplicates out of a delivery that was never in trouble.

Here is the setup, so you can argue with it. One delivery, key evt-1042, a payment confirmation for a single order. A local receiver that sleeps 2.5 seconds before answering 200. A sweeper that ticks every 1.0 second and resends whenever no acknowledgement has arrived. The sender waits up to 4 seconds for each reply, so the first acknowledgement does land, at about 2.5 seconds. I counted duplicates on the receiving side, in the receiver's own log. Then I ran the whole thing twice.

Before the fix After the fix
Sends 3 1
Deliveries the receiver logged 3 1
Extra copies 2 0

Both runs gave the same numbers. Before the fix, the sweeper fired at 0 seconds, at 1 second, and at 2 seconds. The first acknowledgement arrived at 2.5 seconds, a half second after the third copy had already left. After the fix, one send, one delivery, one acknowledgement, and the sweeper spent its next two ticks doing nothing at all. That nothing is the whole point of this piece.

My claim is simple, and I expect some of you to disagree with it. Longer timeouts and longer sweep intervals do not fix webhook duplicates. Only claiming the work once does. Everything else is a new number on the same trap.

Problem 1: silence is not loss

A sweeper that resends on no acknowledgement treats two completely different situations as one. The delivery is gone, or the delivery is slow. From the sender's chair those look identical for the first few seconds. There is no signal in the silence that tells you which one you are in. So the sweeper guesses "lost", because that is the guess a retry loop is built to make. In my run the guess was wrong three times in a row, and each wrong guess was a real copy landing on a real receiver.

People wave this away. "It was only a duplicate, the receiver can ignore it." The receiver in my test was a simple order inbox. It logged three deliveries for one order. If that inbox charges a card, sends a confirmation email, or decrements stock, three deliveries is three of those, unless something downstream catches it. The sweeper created work the receiver never asked for, and then the receiver gets blamed for handling it badly.

Problem 2: the sweeper cannot learn patience from a longer timeout

My first instinct, and probably yours, was to stretch the numbers. Give the sender a longer wait, or the sweeper a longer gap between ticks. I did the arithmetic instead of the change, and the arithmetic is unkind. A 4-second wait already covered the 2.5-second receiver. The timeout was never the problem. The sweeper fired at 1 second and 2 seconds because that is its job: check every second, resend on silence. A longer timeout changes nothing about the second tick.

Stretch the sweep interval instead, say from 1 second to 3 seconds, and this exact receiver stops duplicating. The acknowledgement lands at 2.5 seconds, inside the gap, and the sweeper never fires twice. That feels like a fix. It is a fix for a 2.5-second receiver, on a quiet morning. The next slow day the receiver takes 4 seconds, or 7, or a lock holds it for 12, and the 3-second gap manufactures the same duplicates again. You have not removed the trap. You have moved it to a number you have not hit yet.

Problem 3: every duplicate is a second bill

Count what three deliveries actually cost, even when the receiver is polite enough to ignore two of them. Three sends, three lots of work at the receiving end, three chances for a side effect to slip through. On a busy day that multiplier lands on everything at once, because the slow day is the day every delivery is slow, and the sweeper is resending every one of them. A retry loop that cannot tell slow from lost multiplies the load on the exact receiver that is already struggling, at the exact moment it is struggling. That is a strange way to help.

The fix has to live where the decision lives. The decision is "send this again", and it has to be made once, by one owner, with a record everyone else can see. A longer interval is a hope that the receiver hurries up. A claim is a fact that the work is taken.

Problem 4: a flag in memory is not a claim

The obvious cheap version is a flag in the sender's memory: sending equals true, do not send again. That works until the sender restarts, or until there are two senders, or two copies of the sweeper running side by side, which is exactly how these things end up running. Each one holds its own flag, each one is sure it is the only sender, and the receiver gets two copies anyway. A flag nobody else can see is a private opinion. A claim has to be a shared fact.

So the fix is one row per delivery key, in a table every sender can see, claimed atomically. One row, one key, one owner at a time.

CREATE TABLE claims (
  delivery_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  status TEXT,
  claimed_at REAL
);

The sweeper does not check and then claim. It claims, in one step, and the table decides who won. The insert succeeds for the first caller and fails for everyone else, because the key is the primary key and there can only be one row for it. The winner sends. The losers see status in_flight and skip their tick. When the acknowledgement arrives, the winner marks the row done. A slow run cannot be re-claimed while it is in flight, because the row is already there, already owned, already visible to the next tick.

That is the entire change. Same receiver, same 2.5-second delay, same 1-second sweep, same 4-second wait. Three deliveries became one. The sweeper still ticked every second. It just had nothing to do on the second and third ticks, because the row told it the truth the silence could not: this delivery is already being handled.

Two honest limits, because the test was small. First, this was local: one key, one receiver, no real network, no crash in the middle of a send. A claimer that crashes while holding a row would hold it forever unless the row carries a lease that expires, and I did not test a lease. Do not ship a claim without one. Second, the receiver here was slow, never down. The down case was the previous piece. The slow case is the sneakier of the two, because everything looks fine until you count the copies.

If you run webhooks, you have met this bug, probably on a day you were already busy. What did your duplicate cost you, a double charge, a double email, a customer asking why they got three copies of the same thing? And what fixed it for you, a claim like this one, a key check at the receiving end, or something else entirely?

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: What Makes a Music Box Go 'Tink' (and How to Fake It in Web Audio)
articles.description: What Makes a Music Box Go 'Tink' (and How to Fake It in Web Audio)   A music box is a simple...
articles.body_html:
What Makes a Music Box Go 'Tink' (and How to Fake It in Web Audio)

A music box is a simple machine. A brass cylinder with pins spins against a steel comb. The teeth are cut to different lengths, so each one rings at its own pitch and dies out fast. Long teeth sing low, short teeth sing high. The melody is just the arrangement of pins.

I spent a while rebuilding that machine in a browser: an 18-note virtual music box, C5 to F6, the standard movement size for souvenir boxes. The hard part was never the notes. It was the timbre.

The fourth partial is the whole trick

Pluck one tooth on a real box and you hear three things: a bright fundamental, a very strong fourth partial (four times the fundamental frequency), and a fast decay. The fourth partial is what makes it metallic instead of flutey. A plain sine wave sounds like a test tone. Add its fourth partial, let both decay quickly, and it sounds like a music box.

The voice is three oscillators into one gain:

function playTooth(n, when) {
  const ctx = getCtx();
  const t = when === undefined ? ctx.currentTime : when;
  const f = freqs[n];

  const g = ctx.createGain();
  g.gain.setValueAtTime(0.42, t);
  g.gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(0.001, t + 1.6);

  // fundamental
  const o1 = ctx.createOscillator();
  o1.type = 'sine'; o1.frequency.value = f;

  // the signature: 4th partial, strong but short-lived
  const o2 = ctx.createOscillator();
  o2.type = 'sine'; o2.frequency.value = f * 4;
  const g2 = ctx.createGain();
  g2.gain.value = 0.4;
  g2.gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(0.001, t + 0.9);

  // a faint shimmer one octave above that, gone in 300ms
  const o3 = ctx.createOscillator();
  o3.type = 'sine'; o3.frequency.value = f * 8;
  const g3 = ctx.createGain();
  g3.gain.value = 0.06;
  g3.gain.exponentialRampToValueAtTime(0.001, t + 0.3);

  // steel comb has no low-end mud
  const hp = ctx.createBiquadFilter();
  hp.type = 'highpass'; hp.frequency.value = 300;

  o1.connect(g); o2.connect(g2); g2.connect(g);
  o3.connect(g3); g3.connect(g);
  g.connect(hp); hp.connect(ctx.destination);

  o1.start(t); o2.start(t); o3.start(t);
  o1.stop(t + 1.7); o2.stop(t + 1.0); o3.stop(t + 0.4);
}

The decay envelope does most of the work. The fundamental hangs around for 1.7 seconds; the fourth partial is gone in under one. That gap is the "tink" followed by a fading body. The 300 Hz highpass keeps it from sounding like a soft pad. Music boxes are bright. There's no warmth to protect.

Eighteen teeth, eighteen frequencies:

const teeth = ['C5','C#5','D5','D#5','E5','F5','F#5','G5','G#5','A5','A#5','B5','C6','C#6','D6','D#6','E6','F6'];
const freqs = {};
teeth.forEach(n => {
  const m = n.match(/([A-G])(#?)(\d)/);
  const base = {C:0,D:2,E:4,F:5,G:7,A:9,B:11}[m[1]] + (m[2] === '#' ? 1 : 0);
  const oct = parseInt(m[3]);
  freqs[n] = 440 * Math.pow(2, (base - 9) / 12 + oct - 4);
});

Making it look like a music box, not a keyboard

My first version rendered the 18 teeth as vertical bars in a row. It worked, and it was wrong. A comb isn't a keyboard: it's one steel plate with teeth cut into it, hanging over a cylinder. So I redrew it:

  • One metal spine across the top, teeth hanging down from it. Long teeth on the left (C5, 98 px), stepping down to short teeth on the right (F6, 46 px). Graduated length is the whole instrument.
  • A brass pin cylinder under the teeth tips. The pins are pure CSS, a radial-gradient dot pattern on an 11×12 px tile repeated over a rounded gradient bar.
  • A crank on the right, walnut box, red felt, lid propped open. All divs and gradients. No images, no canvas.

The rotation is the fun part. No WebGL. A rotating cylinder is just the pin pattern's background-position scrolling in a loop:

@keyframes mbspin {
  from { background-position: 0 0; }
  to   { background-position: 0 120px; }
}

The dot tile repeats every 12 px, so 120 px is exactly ten revolutions. Seamless loop, for free. When you pluck one tooth, the cylinder takes a quick quarter turn instead (0 to 32 px in 0.38 s). Re-triggering the same CSS animation per note needs the reflow trick: remove the class, force layout with void el.offsetWidth, add it back. The crank spins while the demo plays, 0.85 s per turn.

Recording without a server

Record stores note events as {f, t} pairs, then replays them through the same voice graph into an OfflineAudioContext:

const off = new OfflineAudioContext(1, len, 44100);
recNotes.forEach(rn => {
  const t = rn.t;
  // ...same gain ramps, same three oscillators, same highpass...
  o1.start(t); o2.start(t); o3.start(t);
  o1.stop(t + 1.7); o2.stop(t + 1.0); o3.stop(t + 0.4);
});
off.startRendering().then(buf => {
  const wav = encodeWav(buf);
  const blob = new Blob([wav], { type: 'audio/wav' });
  download.href = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
});

The WAV encoder is about 40 lines: RIFF header, fmt chunk, PCM16 samples. Because the render runs the same oscillator graph, the export sounds exactly like what you heard live. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Details that mattered more than expected

Plucking fires on mousedown and touchstart, not click. A music box plucks at the press, not the release, and click adds a delay you can feel in fast runs. preventDefault stops the double fire on touch.

Keyboard support maps one key per tooth in pitch order (A W S E D F T G Y H U J K O L P ; '), same layout as the piano tools on the site, so muscle memory carries over.

AudioContext gets created lazily and resumed on the first gesture. Browsers require a gesture before audio starts, and you don't want a suspended context eating your first pluck.

The demo melody is Brahms' Lullaby. Public domain, and the classic music-box tune since 1868.

Fourteen languages, one comb

The tool ships in 14 languages, including RTL (Arabic) and no-space scripts (Thai, Japanese). UI strings come from a per-language file loaded at runtime. The instrument itself is language neutral. The comb renders with dir="ltr" internally so low-to-high tooth order stays physically correct on RTL pages.

What I'd change next

The voice is a model, not a sample. It's small, it loads instantly, and everyone hears the same sound, which is why I kept it synthesized. A version two would add a slightly inharmonic second partial (real teeth aren't perfect sines) and per-tooth detune so chords beat naturally. A sampled comb through a convolution reverb would be closer again. I don't know that I'd want that tradeoff: a few kilobytes of JavaScript vs a sample library.

Try it: soundtool.tools/virtual-music-box. Click the teeth, hit the demo, record something, download the WAV.

I built this tool. It's part of soundtool.tools, a set of browser-based audio utilities.

articles.title: Optimizely Web malware (16 Nov 2026): is your snippet clean? A read-only checker with base64 detection
articles.description: 178 organisations served a crypto clipper, card skimmer and iOS exploit loader through their Optimizely Project JavaScript. A bash checker that pulls your snippet, hunts the IOCs (incl. the base64 loader) and grades your CSP, tested on live snippets and fake infected samples.
articles.body_html:
On 16 November 2026, for about 17 hours, malicious JavaScript ran on the websites of 178 organisations: BBC, CNN, Zoom, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Salesforce and more. Their own sites weren't hacked directly. The attacker rewrote customers' Project JavaScript inside Optimizely Web (the A/B testing platform), and Optimizely's CDN served it to everyone.

The payload swapped crypto wallet addresses, skimmed card numbers, exfiltrated cookies and screenshots, and tried to load an exploit chain on older iPhones.

If your company runs Optimizely Web, you want to know whether your snippet is clean now. I wrote a read-only checker script and tested it against live Optimizely snippets and against harmless fake "infected" samples served from a local web server.

What happened (short version)

From Report URI's write-up (linked below), all times UTC:

  • 04:21 first modified snippet (BBC's) loads a webshell.lol script;
  • from 08:28 the main payload is https://1688360.cc/track.js, rebuilt 26 times during the day, with card skimming added at 13:43;
  • 19:24–19:59 186 of 1,611 checked snippets infected;
  • 23:11 all infected Optimizely files cleaned.

The loader showed up in three forms:

  1. a plain injected <script src="https://1688360.cc/track.js">;
  2. the URL hidden in base64 and decoded with atob(), so grepping for 1688360.cc misses it (Smartsheet was cleaned once and re-infected this way);
  3. the full payload inlined and run via eval, as a fallback if 1688360.cc is blocked.

How the attacker got into Optimizely is not public yet.

Who's affected

  • Site owners using Optimizely Web, including those serving the snippet from their own domain (www.example.com/js/<id>.js): the content still comes from the Optimizely project.
  • Visitors on 16 November, especially:
    • anyone who typed a card into a site's own form (hosted payment iframes like Stripe or Adyen were out of reach);
    • anyone who copied or pasted a crypto address;
    • iPhone/iPad on iOS 18.6 or older, which got the Coruna exploit chain. The visible symptom was the page reloading every 60 seconds.

Check it

Save as optimizely-check.sh, then run bash optimizely-check.sh example.com or pass the project ID: bash optimizely-check.sh 1234567890. Needs bash, curl, grep and sha256sum (Linux, macOS with coreutils, WSL). Messages are Hungarian + English.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# optimizely-check.sh — fertőzött-e az oldalad Optimizely-kódja (2026. november 16-i támadás)?
# Is your site's Optimizely Web snippet carrying the 16 Nov 2026 malware (1688360.cc / webshell.lol)?
# Csak olvas: letölti az oldalt és az Optimizely-snippetet, és IOC-kat keres. Read-only.
#   bash optimizely-check.sh example.com            # főoldal: snippet keresése + CSP-elemzés
#   bash optimizely-check.sh 752092193              # projekt-ID (cdn.optimizely.com/js/<ID>.js)
#   bash optimizely-check.sh https://opt.example.com/js/123.js   # saját domainről kiszolgált snippet
#   DOH=1 bash optimizely-check.sh ...              # ha a saját DNS-szűrőd (Pi-hole, AdGuard) blokkolja az Optimizely-t
# IOC-k forrása / source: https://blog.report-uri.com/worlds-largest-brands-infected-with-malware-via-optimizely/
# MIT license — AikaHub (https://aikahub.com)
set -u
UA="Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/130.0 Safari/537.36"
C=(curl -sS -L -m 30 -A "$UA"); [ "${DOH:-0}" = 1 ] && C+=(--doh-url https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query)
IOC='1688360\.cc|webshell\.lol|linkforge\.cc|5vobauua3ojpklx\.icu|eil786npto9u5bq\.icu|l7bcsnwc7nzr3uo\.icu|je4ft3gn8vxudum\.icu|q1ls1ho9x7wsxlu\.icu|ios-hack\.icu|p55abnw2pnsz0bo\.icu|1y69gy2mdzaltz1\.icu|gm38duxoihbmy5o\.icu|window\._k7|__k7b|02111110|BIGNIAO|aHR0cHM6Ly8xNjg4MzYw|aHR0cHM6Ly93ZWJzaGVsbC5sb2'
BAD_SHA="814a963c0da480e2449d9b6664480156e1cd6d731014117401bf635badec3a0f f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40"
T=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$T"' EXIT
red() { printf '\033[31m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }; grn() { printf '\033[32m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }; ylw() { printf '\033[33m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
RC=0

check_js() {  # $1 = snippet URL
  local u=$1 f="$T/s.js" code
  code=$("${C[@]}" -D "$T/h" -o "$f" -w '%{http_code}' "$u" 2>"$T/err") || { ylw "  ! $u: nem tölthető le ($(tail -c 120 "$T/err" | tr -d '\n'))"; [ "${DOH:-0}" = 1 ] || ylw "    Ha a DNS-szűrőd blokkolja: DOH=1 bash $(basename "$0") ..."; [ "$RC" = 0 ] && RC=2; return; }
  [ "$code" = 200 ] || { ylw "  ! $u: HTTP $code"; return; }
  echo "  snippet: $u"
  echo "    méret/size: $(wc -c <"$f") B · Last-Modified: $(grep -i '^last-modified:' "$T/h" | tail -1 | cut -d' ' -f2- | tr -d '\r')"
  local sha; sha=$(sha256sum "$f" | cut -d' ' -f1); echo "    sha256: $sha"
  case " $BAD_SHA " in *" $sha "*) red "    ✘ ISMERT KÁRTEVŐ (track.js) / known malicious track.js hash"; RC=1 ;; esac
  local hits; hits=$(grep -oE "$IOC" "$f" | sort | uniq -c)
  if [ -n "$hits" ]; then red "    ✘ IOC TALÁLAT / IOC FOUND:"; echo "$hits" | sed 's/^/      /'; RC=1
  else grn "    ✔ nincs ismert IOC / no known IOC"; fi
  local a; a=$(grep -o 'atob(' "$f" | wc -l)
  [ "$a" -gt 0 ] && ylw "    ! atob( ×$a — base64-dekódolás; nézd meg a Project JavaScriptet kézzel (a támadás egyik változata így rejtette a címet)"
}

check_csp() {  # $1 = header file
  local csp; csp=$(grep -i '^content-security-policy:' "$1" | tail -1 | cut -d' ' -f2- | tr -d '\r')
  if [ -z "$csp" ]; then ylw "  CSP: nincs (no Content-Security-Policy header) — a kártevő akadály nélkül futott és küldött volna adatot"; return; fi
  echo "  CSP: $(echo "$csp" | cut -c1-160)$( [ ${#csp} -gt 160 ] && echo …)"
  echo "$csp" | grep -q "script-src" || ylw "    ! nincs script-src (default-src-re esik vissza)"
  echo "$csp" | grep -q "'strict-dynamic'" && ylw "    ! 'strict-dynamic': a megbízott snippet által beszúrt scriptet is engedi (így jutott át a track.js)"
  echo "$csp" | grep -q "'unsafe-eval'" && ylw "    ! 'unsafe-eval': az eval-os, beágyazott tartalékváltozat így is fut"
  echo "$csp" | grep -q "connect-src" && grn "    ✔ van connect-src (a kártya/süti-kiküldést ez fogta meg több helyen)" || ylw "    ! nincs connect-src: a lopott adat bárhová kimehet"
}

[ $# -eq 0 ] && { sed -n '2,9p' "$0"; exit 2; }
for arg in "$@"; do
  echo "== $arg"
  if [[ "$arg" =~ ^[0-9]{6,}$ ]]; then check_js "https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/$arg.js"; continue; fi
  url=$arg; [[ "$url" =~ ^https?:// ]] || url="https://$url"
  if [[ "$url" =~ \.js(\?|$) ]]; then check_js "$url"; continue; fi
  code=$("${C[@]}" -D "$T/ph" -o "$T/p.html" -w '%{http_code}' "$url" 2>"$T/err") || { ylw "  ! nem elérhető: $(tail -c 120 "$T/err")"; RC=2; continue; }
  echo "  oldal/page: HTTP $code, $(wc -c <"$T/p.html") B"
  ph=$(grep -oE "$IOC" "$T/p.html" | sort | uniq -c); [ -n "$ph" ] && { red "  ✘ IOC a HTML-ben / in page HTML:"; echo "$ph" | sed 's/^/    /'; RC=1; }
  check_csp "$T/ph"
  host=$(echo "$url" | sed -E 's#^https?://([^/]+).*#\1#')
  mapfile -t S < <(grep -oE '(https?:)?//(cdn(-pci)?\.optimizely\.com|[a-z0-9.-]+)/js/[0-9]{6,}\.js' "$T/p.html" | sed -E 's#^//#https://#' | sort -u)
  if [ ${#S[@]} -eq 0 ]; then
    ylw "  ? Optimizely-snippet nincs a HTML-ben. Ha tag managerrel / hozzájárulás után töltöd, add meg a projekt-ID-t: bash $(basename "$0") <ID>"
    grep -qi optimizely "$T/p.html" && echo "    (az 'optimizely' szó előfordul az oldalon: $(grep -oi optimizely "$T/p.html" | wc -l)×)"
  fi
  for s in "${S[@]}"; do check_js "$s"; done
done
echo; case $RC in 0) grn "Kész: nincs találat. (Clean.)";; 1) red "Kész: TALÁLAT — lásd fent, és nézd meg az Optimizely Project JavaScriptet.";; *) ylw "Kész: nem minden ellenőrzés futott le.";; esac
exit $RC

What it does:

  • finds the Optimizely snippet in the homepage HTML (cdn.optimizely.com, cdn-pci.optimizely.com, or a self-hosted /js/<number>.js);
  • downloads it and prints size, Last-Modified and SHA-256, and compares the hash to the two published track.js hashes;
  • greps for every attacker domain, the window._k7 / __k7b markers, the iOS loader's 02111110 channel code, and the start of the base64 loader (aHR0cHM6Ly8xNjg4MzYw is https://1688360 in base64);
  • warns on any atob( so you can review it by hand;
  • grades your CSP header against what actually stopped (or didn't stop) this attack.

If the snippet isn't in the HTML (loaded via a tag manager or after cookie consent), pass the project ID. You can find it in the Optimizely UI or in your browser's network tab.

Output on real sites

Peacock, one of the affected sites, this afternoon after the clean-up:

== www.peacocktv.com
  oldal/page: HTTP 200, 152025 B
  CSP: default-src https://*.peacocktv.com; form-action https://*.force.com …
    ! 'unsafe-eval': az eval-os, beágyazott tartalékváltozat így is fut
    ✔ van connect-src (a kártya/süti-kiküldést ez fogta meg több helyen)
  snippet: https://cdn-pci.optimizely.com/js/18154240447.js
    méret/size: 336626 B · Last-Modified: Mon, 16 Nov 2026 21:06:21 GMT
    sha256: bb3c2f9e0d0202e45fd204d819703075432afdef022430512a883adf2750762a
    ✔ nincs ismert IOC / no known IOC

The Last-Modified of 21:06 UTC matches the mass clean-up. The unsafe-eval warning means the inline eval fallback would have run even if track.js had been blocked. Optimizely's own snippet is also clean, with a 21:20 UTC date.

One surprise: on my first run cdn.optimizely.com didn't resolve at all, because our home DNS ad blocker answers 0.0.0.0 for it (cdn-pci.optimizely.com got through, though). That's what the DOH=1 switch is for: it resolves through Cloudflare's DNS-over-HTTPS. As a visitor, that kind of DNS filter was protecting us.

What a hit looks like

All real snippets are clean now, so I tested detection with harmless imitations of the loader forms, served from python3 -m http.server on localhost.

The base64 variant (form 2):

== http://127.0.0.1:8899/js/111111111.js
    ✘ IOC TALÁLAT / IOC FOUND:
            1 aHR0cHM6Ly8xNjg4MzYw
    ! atob( ×1 — base64-dekódolás; nézd meg a Project JavaScriptet kézzel (a támadás egyik változata így rejtette a címet)

Kész: TALÁLAT — lásd fent, és nézd meg az Optimizely Project JavaScriptet.

The plain script-tag variant (form 1):

    ✘ IOC TALÁLAT / IOC FOUND:
            1 1688360.cc
            1 window._k7

A clean script that legitimately uses atob( only gets a warning, not an alert. Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 hit, 2 something couldn't be checked, so you can drop it into cron or CI.

If you get a hit:

  1. Review every project's Project JavaScript and every experiment's custom code in Optimizely for 1688360.cc, atob( and anything you didn't write.
  2. Audit and rotate everything that can write to the account: users, API tokens, integrations.
  3. Treat cards entered in your own forms on 16 November as exposed.
  4. Invalidate session tokens kept in non-HttpOnly cookies.
  5. In the EU, check your GDPR Art. 33 breach-notification duty (72 hours). This is information, not legal advice.

CSP lessons

Report URI checked the response headers of 256 affected organisations. Only 24 (15%) blocked the payload completely.

  • Allowlisting cdn.optimizely.com doesn't help: the malware came from there.
  • 'strict-dynamic' let it through, because the trusted snippet inserted it.
  • With 'unsafe-eval', the inline fallback ran even where track.js was blocked (HSBC).
  • A tight connect-src was worth a lot: no card, cookie or screenshot exfiltration. It did not stop address swapping, which happens inside the page.

Visitors: three quick checks

  1. iPhone/iPad: Settings → General → About → iOS Version. According to the kit's own comments, 18.7.3 and 26.3 (and later) are patched.
  2. Crypto: if you pasted an address on 16 November, verify where the funds went. Attacker addresses include BTC 19g9rZcPeiz8rUvyWpTRyXXhPnjsWrc3kW, ETH/EVM 0xC4026b06D82b0F0B363eda0642D61CfbDc17884e and TRON THvs6p56XkUiMkJeSc51cAP64u2RsTYqxa.
  3. Cards: if you paid in a site's own form that day, watch your statements.

Blocklist for Pi-hole / AdGuard 

1688360.cc
webshell.lol
linkforge.cc
5vobauua3ojpklx.icu
eil786npto9u5bq.icu
l7bcsnwc7nzr3uo.icu
je4ft3gn8vxudum.icu
q1ls1ho9x7wsxlu.icu
ios-hack.icu

I queried them over Cloudflare DoH this afternoon. 1688360.cc and webshell.lol return NXDOMAIN (on hold) and eil786npto9u5bq.icu has no A record. The rest still resolve, including the hard-coded fallback C2s (je4ft3gn8vxudum.icu, q1ls1ho9x7wsxlu.icu, ios-hack.icu), so block them now.

Source: Report URI: World's largest brands infected with malware via Optimizely (IOCs, hashes and timeline).

articles.title: Nobody Runs `npm config list` Before Installing. That's Why the Override Keeps Winning.
articles.description: Yesterday I showed a repo's .npmrc beating my own user config. One line, ignore-scripts=false, in a...
articles.body_html:
Yesterday I showed a repo's .npmrc beating my own user config. One line, ignore-scripts=false, in a folder I had just cloned, switched my protection off, and the install gave me no sign it had happened. The marker file was the only witness. That piece ended with a question I could not answer from memory, and it came from cryptostrapon in the comments: before you install, does npm config list show you the override, and does it say where it came from?

I had a guess. My guess was that it would show the final value and nothing else, a flat list with no blame attached. I ran it instead of arguing from memory, on my own machine, node v24.22.1 and npm 10.9.4, with the same test package and the same setup as yesterday: a user config saying ignore-scripts=true, a repo config saying false, and a hook that writes a marker file if it runs.

My claim, before the numbers: the four-second check that would have caught yesterday's override is not a nice habit for careful people. It is the only honest answer npm gives you about what it is about to do, and the reason nobody runs it is not that it is slow or hidden. It is that nothing in the way we install ever asks for it.

Problem 1: the check works, and it is better than the question promised

I ran npm config list inside the repo folder, before installing anything. Here is what came back, word for word:

; "user" config from /home/hatch/workspace/aheadkit-traffic-programme/content-daily/2026-11-18/runs/npm-config-list/fake-home/.npmrc

; ignore-scripts = true ; overridden by project

; "project" config from /home/hatch/workspace/aheadkit-traffic-programme/content-daily/2026-11-18/runs/npm-config-list/repo/.npmrc

ignore-scripts = false

Read that again. It does not just give the final value. It shows my user value, true, then stamps it overridden by project, then names the project file by its full path, then gives the winning value, false. Layer name and file path, both, in plain text. I asked whether the flip is visible and whether it names the file it came from. The answer to both is yes, and it volunteers the word "overridden" without being asked.

And the timing embarrasses the premise of the question. The lead that prompted this piece called it a four-second check. The measured time was 0.179 seconds. The control run in a folder with no repo config took 0.171 seconds. A repeat inside the repo gave the identical output and the same effective value, false. The check is not four seconds. It is a fifth of a second, and it hands you the name of the file that beat you.

Then I installed, to close the loop. The check had said false. The hook ran, and the marker file was written at 2026-11-18T00:06:02.883Z. The control install, in the folder with no repo config, wrote no marker at all. The check predicted the install exactly, because the check and the install read the same layers.

Problem 2: the check only works if you run it inside the folder

This is the catch, and it is a real one. I ran the same command from the parent folder, one level above the repo, with everything else identical. The output showed my user value, true, and nothing else. No project section, no override, no hint that a file one folder down disagrees with me.

; "user" config from /home/hatch/workspace/aheadkit-traffic-programme/content-daily/2026-11-18/runs/npm-config-list/fake-home/.npmrc

ignore-scripts = true

The project layer only exists when your working folder is inside the project. Run the check from your home folder, or from the folder where you keep all your clones, and it tells you a true thing about the wrong place. It says your protection is on, and it is right, for the folder you are standing in. The repo you are about to install is not that folder.

That is a small detail with a large consequence. A check that has to be run in the right folder is a check that fails silently when you run it in the wrong one, which is the same failure mode as the override itself. The tool answers honestly. It answers about where you are, not about where you are going.

Problem 3: the command most of us know answers a different question

If you have ever checked an npm setting, you probably used npm config get. I did too. Inside the repo it says false. In the clean folder it says true. Correct both times, and useless in exactly the way that matters: it gives the value and no source. A false from config get could be your own choice, a project file, or a default you never set. You cannot tell which, and the difference between those three is the whole story.

The JSON form is no better. npm config list --json in the repo shows "ignore-scripts": false and names no file at all. The plain list is the only form that shows the layers, the file paths, and the word "overridden". The prettiest output is the least useful one here. That is a small, annoying truth about this tool, and it is the kind of thing you only learn by running both forms side by side.

Where I ran the check Effective value Did it name the file?
Inside the repo folder false Yes, full project path, plus "overridden by project"
Inside a folder with no repo config true Nothing to name
From the parent folder, outside the repo true No, the project layer was invisible
npm config get inside the repo false No, value only
npm config list --json inside the repo false No, value only

Problem 4: nobody runs it because nothing asks for it

So the check is fast, it names the file, and it predicts the install. Why did I never run it before yesterday? I have an honest answer, and it is not a flattering one.

Installing has a shape, and the shape has no gap in it for a check. Clone, install, watch the output, move on. The check belongs before the install, and before the install there is nothing to look at yet, no error, no warning, no reason to pause. A protection that fails silently creates no moment that asks to be checked. You feel safe, and feeling safe is the opposite of a prompt.

There is a second reason, quieter. npm config list sounds like a command for debugging npm itself, not for checking a repo you just cloned. It reads like something you run when installs are broken, not something you run when installs look fine. And installs that look fine are exactly the ones carrying an override, because an override does not break the install. It just changes what the install is allowed to do.

I am not going to pretend I will now run this before every install. I will not. What I will do is narrower and, I think, more honest: for a repo I do not know well, I run it inside the folder before the install, and I read the two lines that matter, the user value and the project value. A fifth of a second, and I know which file won. For a repo I know and trust, I skip it, and I skip it knowing I skipped it, which is a different thing from never having thought about it.

Problem 5: the honest limit of the check

Two limits, because the test was small. First, the check is a snapshot. It shows the config at the moment you run it. It says nothing about a repo whose config changes between the check and the install, and it says nothing about code that runs on first load, which no install setting touches at all. The check answers one question, whether the repo disagrees with your user config right now, and it answers it well. It is not a verdict on the repo.

Second, the check only helps if you read it. The output is short, but the two lines that matter sit among lines about node versions and folder paths, and a tired eye can slide past them. The tool did its part. It printed the file path and the word "overridden". The rest is on the person reading.

So the claim stands, with one correction. cryptostrapon's question pointed at a four-second check. It is not four seconds. It is under a fifth of a second, it names the file that beat your setting, and it predicts the install. The reason it never gets run is not cost. It is that the install gives you no moment to run it in, and the command sounds like it belongs to a different problem. Fix the moment, not the tool: run it inside the folder, before the install, when the repo is one you have not vetted yet.

Have you ever run npm config list before an install and caught something? Or caught a project file undoing one of your own settings in some other tool, and only found out later? I would like to hear what it was, and whether you check first now or still trust the setting and move on.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam
